[ManuscriptTitle] ChandRush Chapter 02 Manuscript
[ManuscriptSubtitle] The Feast That Would Not Share
[ProductionLabel] Integrated manuscript V04 • 21 October 2026
[ProductionNote] Mathematics: Fractions, Decimals and Percentages. Complete Chapter 02 story and supplied Friendly Teacher Draft 10 Revised, prepared for subsequent pagination and panelisation.
[ProductionHeading] Reading and using this manuscript
[ProductionNote] All Scene, Visual beat, Location, Teaching block and Companion inset identifiers are production references, not graphic-novel page or panel numbers. The Word pages are review pages. Final page assignments, panel dimensions, typography and placement belong to later stages.
[ProductionNote] Production notes and field labels are non-printing. Each CAPTION TEXT field contains printable narration for its immediately preceding visual beat. Consecutive narration paragraphs within one caption group share that visual; a paragraph break alone does not request a new image. Caption groups separated by dialogue retain their source reading order.
[ProductionNote] Each SPEECH BUBBLE TEXT field contains only the approved words for that balloon. Print only its Dialogue Copy paragraph. Speaker names, tail targets, addressees, source attributions, beat headings and staging are metadata: never prepend or append them to a speech bubble. A name actually spoken within a line remains part of that line. Bare “says”, “asks” and “replies” attributions are retained only in metadata. Meaningful action narration remains printable. Outer prose quotation marks are omitted; attribution commas become full stops. One interrupted grammatical question in Scene CH02 08A is rejoined into a single question without changing its words.
[ProductionNote] Separate speaking beats are distinct drawable moments. Retain the explicitly named camera, background, foot positions and prop states, then apply the current beat’s pose, gaze, expression and action. Do not reset a held object or equipment state merely because a new beat begins. Silent beats provide necessary physical transitions without invented dialogue or captions.
[ProductionNote] Static-image rule: each Visual beat describes one frozen drawable moment. Background context may explain what has already happened or what follows between images; illustrate only the assigned moment. Do not combine a character’s successive poses or locations in one image. Captions may describe an action across that moment without requiring animated motion. Keep the story narration and dialogue in their supplied order; past references within dialogue remain meaningful past references.
[ProductionNote] SURFACE TEXT belongs only to the named note or sign. Source narration that mentions a label remains narration; any required visible label must match its exact supplied wording and quantity. Do not put note text into Pip’s speech: Pip transports written messages and does not supply unseen answers.
[ProductionNote] The friendly teacher narrator addresses the reader directly. Teaching headings, explanations, examples, questions, working, answers, tables, diagrams and their supplied captions are printable. Paragraphs explicitly labelled Production note remain non-printing. Preserve each question before its solution, keeping required figures with it and avoiding answers in unsolved question visuals. Technical figure identifiers such as V03a-R7 are non-printing metadata only. A caption’s reader-facing sentence is unchanged. Preserve mathematical Figure 1, Figure 2 and similar labels used by the lesson itself.
[ProductionNote] Location masters below fix physical geography. Each sequence and scene identifies the relevant master, visible anchors and current state. For a scene split across pages, pagination must copy the applicable non-printing location, camera, positions, props, equipment state, text-ownership and visual requirements onto every receiving page. Resolve explicit references to their detailed source, carry only the named elements and retain the receiving beat’s changes. Character appearance descriptions need not be repeated: the one opening register and approved character assets govern identity.
[ProductionNote] Cross-references point to named Locations, Scenes or Visual beats, never “the page above” or an unnamed preceding view. A reverse angle changes screen positions, not physical left and right. Character-and-scenery insets are independent companion moments at completed teaching boundaries; they do not advance the plot or change equipment.
[ProductionNote] The reader can pause and return to a lesson without changing the adventure’s clock. Do not invent a time-freezing device or turn the teaching into a speed test. No attraction opens for public play before the Moon Bell’s welcome ring.
[ProductionHeading] Continuity at the opening
[ProductionNote] Chapter 01 has repaired Lantern Street. Its arches are lit and moonline continuous. Food Street has just been revealed, with its entrance obstructed by the crooked cart and trapped bowl; its serving equipment remains wrong. Chapter 02 starts by clearing that obstruction, not by replaying the prologue or any Chapter 01 repair.
[ProductionNote] Ahana carries the brass work lamp in her right hand at the opening; her cream sketchbook and ordinary pencil are packed. Tara has just received the evidence sleeve in her left hand and holds her staff in her right. The first silent beat places the lamp safely on the near packing bench and secures the sleeve in Tara’s sash pocket before either character needs those hands.
[ProductionNote] The trio’s silver invitations bear blue volunteer seals and remain secured. Tez retains the same faded pale-grey stripe patches seen at the end of Chapter 01; repairing food service does not restore them. The Moon Bell is still missing, the dust’s cause is unknown, and Veer’s adult face and motive have not been revealed.
[ProductionNote] Ira, Kabir, the girl in green and her friends are outside the Gate. The first sixteen-drink order and the later forty/twenty-two admission groups are separate lists. The trio are working volunteers outside those sixty-two guests. The chapter ends at the open Parade threshold, before its repairs and Veer’s present-day appearance.
[ProductionHeading] Character register — non-printing, once for the chapter
[ProductionNote] Author’s appearance rule: all human characters have fair skin, including the trio, Tara, Ira, Kabir, the girl in green, her friends, background visitors and the children in the photograph. This overrides older skin descriptions. Tez retains fur; the helpers and clown retain their wooden material. Use the approved character assets by name in later scenes. No character or location reference-image generation is part of this manuscript.
[BeatHeading] Ahana
[ProductionNote] Eleven; fair skin, expressive dark eyes and short loose black curls. Teal jacket over burnt-orange shirt, charcoal cargo trousers, blue-and-white trainers and navy backpack. Notices people and arrangements, writes the delivery request and helps actively. Sketchbook stays packed throughout this chapter. Her lamp rests at the packing bench during work and is retrieved before the Parade threshold.
[BeatHeading] Vihaan
[ProductionNote] Eleven; fair skin, lively dark eyes and short side-swept black hair. Mustard-yellow jacket, navy shirt and trousers, light trainers and red backpack. His invitation stays secured. He approves an estimate too soon, acknowledges it and later makes an independent sound check. Preserve both his humour and competence.
[BeatHeading] Navya
[ProductionNote] Eleven; fair skin, dark eyes and two practical black braids. Burgundy overshirt over striped ivory top, blue cargo jeans, pale trainers and tan cross-body satchel with a small tool pouch. She checks and changes safe settings, records quantities and directs the balancing move. No ankle injury in this chapter.
[BeatHeading] Tara
[ProductionNote] Elderly, tall and broad-shouldered; fair skin, alert face and long silver-white braid. Indigo robe with restrained gold embroidery, ivory inner clothes, teal sash, practical dark footwear and approved jewellery. Dark wooden staff with its familiar brass Moon Bell ornament. Usually staff in right hand, left free; explicitly support the staff at the wall for two-handed box and writing work. The staff ornament is not the stolen Moon Bell.
[BeatHeading] Tez
[ProductionNote] Orange tiger cub with cream muzzle, cheeks, chest and paws; blue stripes with the established faded pale-grey patches; navy scarf and moon clasp. Four-pawed anatomy and below-knee scale. Expressive ears, tail and gaze; no human hands, tool grip or heavy carrying. Food jokes do not change orders or portions.
[BeatHeading] Ira
[ProductionNote] Nine; fair skin, oval face, dark eyes, straight black hair in a short ponytail. Pale powder-blue jacket over ivory, charcoal leggings, white trainers and small cream cross-body purse. Connects the written list to real waiting people. She keeps her original cup drawing after its return; later notes use new sheets.
[BeatHeading] Kabir
[ProductionNote] Twelve; fair skin, slightly taller than the trio, lean build, short thick black hair. Rust hoodie, dark joggers, pale trainers and black wristwatch. His ruled notebook and pencil fit in his pocket. Usually notebook left, pencil right while recording; he can put both away. He knows only what he sees or is told.
[BeatHeading] Girl in green and friends
[ProductionNote] The girl is eight, fair-skinned, with chin-length black hair, two yellow clips, green hoodie, dark trousers and light trainers. Keep her two established friends together; one has a yellow water bottle. They remain recognisable across food, drink and admission cutaways. Background guests are children aged eight to thirteen in contemporary urban casual clothing.
[BeatHeading] Wooden helpers
[ProductionNote] Honey-coloured carved figures, visible grain, painted eyes, round brass joints, broad wooden feet and separate wooden thumbs. Broad blue-waistcoated helper with navy sash: carrying, table work and first trolley delivery. Green helper: Gate. Main food helper: saffron apron and ivory cap, controls cooking. Two smaller assistants: saffron waistbands, alternate delivery, drinks and packing. “Drink assistant” is one of these two, not a third identical worker. Establish returns before reassigning an assistant; never duplicate one helper across locations.
[BeatHeading] Pip
[ProductionNote] Palm-sized brass bird, rounded body, copper wing plates, glass-blue eyes, pointed beak, gripping feet and one spring clip below its beak. Carries one folded note at a time; it can fly ahead of a trolley but cannot carry food, tools or the Bell. No unsupplied speech.
[BeatHeading] The real wooden clown
[ProductionNote] Tall, slender wooden performer; ivory-painted face, round red nose, blue carved curls and eyebrows, brass wrists and striped oversized shoes. Red jacket with blue sleeves, checked trousers and pointed red-and-gold hat. Appears only in the final yard reveal, hands lost inside oversized sleeves. He does not speak; no disguise reveal or nose-tap greeting yet.
[BeatHeading] The photograph
[ProductionNote] Tara beside exactly three children. Veer is twelve; his face is scratched away and only his name identifies him. The other two are unnamed. All pictured humans have fair skin. Do not invent Veer’s missing face, show his adult face or add a separate flashback. The photograph remains inside its blue-lidded box.
[ProductionHeading] Location masters — fixed geography and changing states
[ProductionNote] These full descriptions are non-printing production context. V16 supplies the physical locations and state constraints. Scene beats control when each state becomes visible. Later production should carry the relevant master and current scene notes forward, without carrying future answers into an earlier scene.
[ProductionHeading] Location CH02 L01 Food Street — Master from Lantern Street
[ProductionNote] A covered lane beneath saffron and teal awnings opens beyond Lantern Street’s shutters. The recipe and cooking counter is on the left; jugs and the juice urn are on the right. The near packing bench has a side door to Return Walk. A round two-tray loading table sits in the central clear lane.
[ProductionNote] The far opening leads to the Parade Ground. The initial obstruction is one crooked cart with a bowl under its wheel. The food helper wears a saffron apron and ivory cap; two smaller assistants deliver food. The main cooking surface is behind the counter, beyond the children’s hands. The sixteen-cup trolley waits at the packing end. No human cooks or hidden extra kitchen are introduced.
[ProductionNote] Required views. Threshold wide; separate recipe, drinks and packing counter views; central loading-table medium. The waiting Gate crowd is shown in its own cutaway, never behind the cooking counter.
[ProductionNote] Continuity implementation. The physical left/right convention is always the view from Lantern Street towards the Parade Ground. Return Walk follows the fair’s left boundary, so its side doorway and the near packing bench belong to that physical-left entrance zone. Park the cleared crooked cart against the near-left wall before the bench, leaving both doorways and the central route clear. The broad helper’s ordinary handcart and the sixteen-cup delivery trolley are separate vehicles. Warm task lamps light hands; cool full-moon light edges canopy gaps. Lantern Street stays repaired behind the entrance.
[ProductionHeading] Location CH02 L02 Food Street — Recipe Counter and Dosa Dispenser
[ProductionNote] The pale left-hand counter has an original recipe book, balance, fractional weights and labelled covered bowls. A brass batter tank and adjustable measuring cup stand behind its cool working edge, above a cooking plate. A separate dry shelf holds finished plates.
[ProductionNote] The stock label 1¾ kg = 7/4 kg belongs to a weighed tray. The false 5/4 kg stock label does not control the serving dose. The recipe for one full dosa is 1/6 kg of batter; the physical portion stop controls that measuring cup. A cold test goes into a bowl with heat off. The food helper handles the hot plate and cooked food. The next corrected pour fits the next plate; an already cooked dosa never shrinks. Wrap filling is a separate checked stock.
[ProductionNote] Required views. Overhead book/weights insert; stock-card versus portion-stop close-ups; cold test with tap shut; safe side view of next pour and separate finished-dosa result. Do not put batter directly on a serving plate.
[ProductionNote] Continuity implementation. Its blue timber wall, brass tank base and pale front edge remain anchors in close-ups. The stock-card clip belongs to the weighed tray; it is not the measuring-cup portion stop. The supply/shut-off control is accessible from the cool end. Tara can reach it with her left hand while holding her staff right. Cold checks occur with heat OFF; only the food helper handles hot surfaces and cooked food. The lamp above the work area is fixed. Ahana’s portable lamp rests at the near packing bench during the counter work.
[ProductionNote] Dispenser control reference: the supply tap isolates the brass tank from the measuring cup. The cup’s adjustable stop sets its fill capacity, calibrated in batter mass for this recipe. The long cool-side handle operates the cup outlet; a mechanical interlock closes the tank feed before opening that outlet. At rest the outlet is closed; the supply tap may charge the cup. Lowering the handle isolates the tank and releases only the cup contents. The heater is independent. Use these same three controls in every view. For the cold flow trial only, the measuring cup swings aside on its cleaning hinge while heat is OFF. This exposes the tank’s supply spout directly above the trial bowl; Tara’s supply tap therefore starts and stops that flow without using the cup handle or interlock. The helper holds the cup safely aside. Reseat the empty cup before the new measured batch; the serving stop is not validated by this trial. The tank and cup start empty after the earlier faulty cooking; do not imply a hidden batter quantity. The original stock tray and the separate wrap-filling vessels remain distinct.
[ProductionHeading] Location CH02 L03 Food Street — Packing Bench and Balanced Loading Table
[ProductionNote] A near-entrance shelf and pale packing bench sit beside the Return Walk door. Ira’s small cup drawing clips above the bench. The delivery trolley has sixteen cup places in its upper carrier and a separate lower snack shelf, marked MAXIMUM LOAD 4.5 kg. Its empty snack tray weighs 0.5 kg. Each sealed fruit-and-cracker pack weighs 0.22 kg. The circular loading table has two matching trays equally far from its centre.
[ProductionNote] Thirty-six ready packs plus four recovered behind the entrance cart make forty. They are a distinct batch from freshly cooked wraps and dosas. Sixteen packs plus their empty tray have mass 4.02 kg, below the lower shelf’s 4.5 kg limit; the helper also inspects the shelf. The 40% first-trip share is not supplied before T2.10. Twenty-four packs remain for later deliveries. The separate loading table begins at 25 and 15 equal-mass packs; moving five gives 20 and 20. Taking eight from each leaves 12 and 12. Ira’s original drawing travels from the packing bench to the Gate on the first trolley. Ira keeps it in her purse there; it does not return to Food Street with the empty trolley. Later messages use new paper.
[ProductionNote] Required views. Order-board medium; recovered four-pack tray insert; overhead two-tray count diagram; separate first delivery leaving Return Walk and arriving at the Gate.
[ProductionNote] Continuity implementation. The upper carrier is a four-by-four arrangement of sixteen cup places. The lower shelf’s MAXIMUM LOAD 4.5 kg label belongs only to that shelf. The single removable snack tray weighs 0.5 kg. The table has a fixed pedestal, a rotating head and a centrally pivoted two-tray cradle. Its one accessible brake housing has a rotation latch and a squeeze lever linked to the cradle’s tilt damper. The latch holds rotation from Visual beat CH02 01B C to CH02 13D A; it does not clamp the cradle. Squeezing the lever damps sudden tilt while held; it does not rigidly lock the cradle angle. Tara holds that lever in CH02 13B B and CH02 13C. The same damping allows slow, controlled settling as loads become equal, so the cradle levels at 20/20 without releasing the rotation latch. Mechanical travel stops limit the dip; no tray falls. At the opening both trays are empty and the unladen cradle rests at its shallow low stop from earlier handling. Do not add undiscovered snack packs to explain this opening angle. The forty-pack load appears only in CH02 13B. After 12/12 is established, Tara releases the squeeze lever and rotation latch in CH02 13D A. The original cup drawing is clipped above the bench from Scene CH02 02D until Scene CH02 14A. After dispatch its former clip is empty. Use exact dedicated count diagrams for the pack states; do not demand tiny exact counts in every scenic wide.
[ProductionHeading] Location CH02 L04 Old Blue Gate — Exterior Waiting Lane
[ProductionNote] Two enormous weathered blue timber doors stand between pale-stone piers. Brass ribs and moon-shaped openings decorate the doors. A round full-moon ornament hangs above. Seen from outside, a small service door is cut into the left door leaf. A bench is on the right and a planter on the left.
[ProductionNote] The separate equipment exit is farther left beyond the stone pier. It is not the child-height door in the large leaf. Children aged eight to thirteen wait in contemporary urban casual clothing. Use a few foreground groups and a suggested crowd; do not render three hundred individually countable people. Ira, Kabir and the girl in green remain identifiable. Tara does not meet the trio outside. The Bell is never mounted on the Gate arch.
[ProductionNote] Required views. Arrival wide from the lane; bench/planter medium; invitation close-up; low Tez doorway view. Gate ornaments and invitations have bright, fading and restored-light states without changing their shapes.
[ProductionNote] Continuity implementation. The equipment exit beyond the exterior-left pier is a different route. The Bell is absent from Entry Court and is never mounted on the Gate arch. Gate cutaways show actual waiting children and helpers, not the trio magically relocated from Food Street. Before the final authorisation, food passes through the supervised service doorway while general admission waits. The first forty later wait inside Entry Court; Ira, Kabir and the girl in green with her two friends remain among the next twenty-two. Keep contemporary urban clothing and full-moon-night light.
[ProductionHeading] Location CH02 L05 Food Street — Drink and Weighing Counter
[ProductionNote] The right-hand pale counter holds equal-capacity recipe jugs, a broad marked juice urn, a capped reserve bottle and a small measuring jug. The work lamp is above-left. Dry records and an ingredient scale occupy the end away from the pour.
[ProductionNote] The recipe jugs show ¾ L/0.75 L and 0.7 L. The delivery urn begins at 3.9 L. The reserve bottle has 1 L capacity: its earlier preparation record starts at 0.85 L and records a 0.25 L withdrawal, leaving 0.60 L when it is brought to the urn. One new 0.10 L transfer makes the urn 4 L and leaves 0.50 L in the bottle. The combined bottle change is −0.35 L. Sixteen cups each receive 0.25 L. A separate ingredient packet marked 0.6 kg is 600 g. T2.8 uses a 50% fill card for the half-full bottle. T2.9 uses the assistant’s one-litre mixing jug and its ¾-of-capacity refill line, written as 75% on the matching board. These capacity shares are distinct from T2.10’s 16-of-40 snack count. No two-dial siphon or extra pour is added.
[ProductionNote] Required views. Jug comparison; bottle preparation record and current amounts; measured transfer and separate result; dry kg/g packet; snack-shelf limit and tray-mass diagram; bottle and mixing-jug fill cards in distinct close-ups. Show exact cup or pack counts only in the relevant diagram, not every wide.
[ProductionNote] Continuity implementation. The recipe jugs’ top-up uses the assistant’s pouring pot. The urn top-up uses one measured 0.10 L from the reserve bottle. Do not combine those supplies or operations. The reserve bottle and the later one-litre mixing jug are different containers. After the sixteen quarter-litre cups have been filled, the urn’s first 4 L has been dispensed; later records can show the earlier post-transfer 4 L, but later scenery must not duplicate that liquid. The approved reveal timing shows 0.50 L after T2.7A and reserves the combined −0.35 L change for T2.7C.

[ProductionNote] A pale paved passage with indigo posts and a blue timber roof runs along the fair’s left boundary. The outer wall is on one side; the open side faces the fair. Warm bracket lamps mark a clear route wide enough for a handcart and escort.
[ProductionNote] Entry Court is at one end; Moon Square and the Tower arcade are at the other. Food Street’s side delivery doorway opens onto the middle. It does not contain the roof lift. A travel picture should show a few posts and the destination doorway relevant to that movement, not both distant courtyards at once.
[ProductionNote] Required views. Directional travel inserts towards Entry Court, Food Street or Moon Square. Keep the named destination and the latest light state explicit.
[ProductionNote] Continuity implementation. Food Street’s side delivery door opens onto its middle; Entry Court and the Gate are in one direction, Moon Square and the Tower arcade in the other. This chapter’s delivery travels towards Entry Court. A travel image shows only the relevant stretch and destination doorway. It does not contain the roof freight lift or turn into the separate equipment passage. The first trolley travels out with the broad helper and returns before the assistants take over.
[ProductionHeading] Location CH02 L07 Parade Ground — Rehearsal Yard and Visitor Lane
[ProductionNote] A broad yard beyond Food Street contains an empty rehearsal loop. A roped pedestrian lane follows its left edge to the Moon Square counting arch. The elephant work area and temporary supports are on the right. A costume bench is beside the lane but outside the moving loop.
[ProductionNote] An equipment gallery crosses the upper-right background, with a near stair and far staff door. A rear walkway from that door reaches the back of the counting arch. That explains Veer’s later movement. The forty-person group passes along the protected left lane; the following twenty-two wait at the viewing rope until the float test finishes. No public parade begins before the Bell.
[ProductionNote] Required views. Wide from Food Street; separate gallery view; roped-group medium; float support view; counting-arch rear close-up. Do not compress the float and arch theft into one simultaneous picture of Ahana seeing both.

[SequenceHeading] Sequence 01 A kitchen with conflicting instructions
[ProductionLabel] Production sequence reference CH02-01. Non-printing background and continuity.
[ProductionNote] Background — Location CH02 L01. Food Street’s covered lane has saffron and teal awnings, the recipe/cooking counter on physical left, jugs and juice urn on physical right, a near packing bench beside the Return Walk doorway, a central circular two-tray table and far shutters towards the Parade Ground.
[ProductionNote] Background — Location CH02 L02. The pale physical-left recipe counter has a cupboard beneath, a dry book-and-balance work area (equipment remains in the cupboard until Visual beat CH02 01G A), a brass batter tank and adjustable measuring cup behind the cool working edge, a separate cooking plate behind the guard and a dry shelf for finished plates.
[ProductionNote] Background — Location CH02 L03. The near-entrance pale packing bench and stock shelf stand beside the Return Walk doorway. [SceneHeading] Scene CH02 01A Clear the entrance
[ProductionLabel] Production instructions are non-printing. Exact reader text is assigned beneath each visual beat.
[ProductionNote] Setting. Location CH02 L01: Food Street’s covered lane has saffron and teal awnings, the recipe/cooking counter on physical left, jugs and juice urn on physical right, a near packing bench beside the Return Walk doorway, a central circular two-tray table and far shutters towards the Parade Ground. Same full-moon night. Warm task lamps and cool moonlit edges remain consistent; the current scene controls repaired and unrepaired states.
[ProductionNote] View. Wide from restored Lantern Street into Food Street: recipe counter physical left, drinks right, near-left packing bench and Return Walk door, round table central and closed Parade shutters far ahead.
[ProductionNote] Cast and positions. Ahana and Navya stand either side of the obstructing cart; Vihaan is beside its trapped wheel. Tara waits at the threshold with staff right and evidence sleeve left. Tez is behind Ahana, out of the wheel path. The blue-waistcoated helper waits outside with its empty handcart.
[ProductionNote] Props and state progression. The bowl is trapped under one cart wheel. The obstructing cart and the broad helper’s empty handcart are different objects. At the opening Ahana still carries the brass lamp in her right hand; her left is free. The cleared cart will park against the near-left wall, short of the packing bench and clear of the Return Walk door.
[ProductionNote] Planning requirements. Preserve the final Chapter 01 threshold. Lantern Street stays lit. Food Street is powered for work; the fair has not opened. Show the hand-freeing action before the push.

The cup’s adjustable stop sets its fill capacity, calibrated in batter mass for this recipe. The long cool-side handle operates the cup outlet; a mechanical interlock closes the tank feed before opening that outlet. At rest the outlet is closed; the supply tap may charge the cup. Location CH02 L02: The pale physical-left recipe counter has a cupboard beneath, a dry book-and-balance work area (equipment remains in the cupboard until Visual beat CH02 01G A), a brass batter tank and adjustable measuring cup behind the cool working edge, a separate cooking plate behind the guard and a dry shelf for finished plates. Same full-moon night. Warm task lamps and cool moonlit edges remain consistent; the current scene controls repaired and unrepaired states.
[ProductionNote] View. Medium of the measuring cup and its accessible side controls, with the food helper behind and Tara at the shut-off end; retain a strip of cool counter in the foreground.

The original book, balance and fractional weights remain stored inside the closed cupboard until Visual beat CH02 01G A; batter and wrap filling are separate foods in separate vessels. The cooking plate is behind the counter. Ahana’s lamp rests on the near packing bench; her sketchbook is packed. Tara’s evidence sleeve is secured in her sash pocket. No character reaches over the hot plate. The helper’s two cards lie flat at the dry end. The measuring-cup stop is still wrong. Supply tap begins open and is closed in beat C; heat is switched off before any later cold test.

[ProductionNote] Dispenser control reference: the supply tap isolates the brass tank from the measuring cup. The cup’s adjustable stop sets its fill capacity, calibrated in batter mass for this recipe. The long cool-side handle operates the cup outlet; a mechanical interlock closes the tank feed before opening that outlet. At rest the outlet is closed; the supply tap may charge the cup. Lowering the handle isolates the tank and releases only the cup contents. The heater is independent. Use these same three controls in every view. [PanelizationMetadata] SOURCE: Global production rules — Static-image rule: each Visual beat describes one frozen drawable moment.
[PanelizationMetadata] APPLIES TO: CH02-PAGE006-PANEL02; Visual beat CH02 01G B; assigned moment only
[ProductionNote] Static-image rule: each Visual beat describes one frozen drawable moment. Background context may explain what has already happened or what follows between images; illustrate only the assigned moment. Do not combine a character’s successive poses or locations in one image. Captions may describe an action across that moment without requiring animated motion. Keep the story narration and dialogue in their supplied order; past references within dialogue remain meaningful past references.

Now Grandpa has a box of 12 pies. He wants to give away 3/4 of those 12 pies. This time, “the whole” means all 12 pies together. We will divide the group, not cut each pie.
Look at the picture: each small circle represents 1 pie. The 4 boxes put the 12 pies into 4 equal groups. Each group contains 3 pies.
[ProductionLabel] DO NOT PRINT — Figure reference: V02 | The following caption sentence is printable unchanged.
[Caption] The whole group contains 12 pies. Each of its four equal groups contains 3 pies.
[ProductionNote] Production note V02 — Show 12 equal labelled pie symbols arranged as four visibly separated groups of three. Mark three groups teal, one unfilled; do not depict 3/4 of a single pie. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
Find 1/4 of the 12 pies: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 pies.
We need 3/4, so take 3 of those groups: 3 × 3 = 9 pies.
We can record both steps as 3/4 × 12 = 9 pies.
Grandpa gives away 9 pies. Check: 3 pies stay in the box, and 9 + 3 = 12 pies.
Notice the difference: 1/4 of 1 pie is a piece of pie, but 1/4 of 12 pies is 3 pies. Before using a fraction, say what you are taking a fraction of.
Next we will count amounts such as 1 whole pie and half of another pie. Later we will write amounts as decimals and percentages too. Keep a pencil nearby. At each “Your turn”, try the question before reading its worked answer.

[PanelizationLabel] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
# 2.1 Improper Fractions and Mixed Numbers
The rectangles in the next picture stand for pies. Each full rectangle is 1 whole pie, cut into 2 equal halves. A shaded half-rectangle means 1/2 of a pie.
On the left, we have 1 whole pie and 1/2 of another pie. Let’s count how many half-pies that makes.
[ProductionLabel] DO NOT PRINT — Figure reference: V03 | The following caption sentence is printable unchanged.
[Caption] 1 whole pie gives 2 halves; another half makes 3 halves.
[ProductionNote] Production note V03 — Show identical wholes. First state has one complete whole and one half; second state shows exactly three half-pieces. Label 1 1/2 and 3/2. Keep the reference whole fixed. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
The first whole pie gives us 2 halves: 1 = 2/2.
The second pie gives us 1 more half: 1/2.
Count the halves: 2 + 1 = 3 half-pies.
So 1 1/2 = 2/2 + 1/2 = 3/2.
Read that as “one and a half pies is the same amount as three half-pies”. We have not gained or lost any pie.
Look at 3/2. The bottom number, 2, tells us that each whole pie is cut into 2 equal parts. The top number, 3, tells us that we have 3 of those parts. The bottom number is called the denominator; the top number is the numerator.
A fraction such as 1/2 or 3/4 is less than 1 whole. Its top number is smaller than its bottom number. We call it a proper fraction.
A fraction such as 3/2 is more than 1 whole. The fraction 4/4 is exactly 1 whole. When the top number is greater than or equal to the bottom number, we call it an improper fraction. “Improper” does not mean the fraction has misbehaved!
The number 1 1/2 has a whole-number part, 1, and a fraction part, 1/2. That is why we call it a mixed number. It means 1 + 1/2, not 1 × 1/2.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE014-PANEL01

## Changing the way we count
Let’s change 2 3/4 into a fraction. Imagine 2 whole pies and 3/4 of another pie. In the next picture, each full rectangle represents 1 pie cut into 4 equal parts. Each small part is one quarter, 1/4, of a pie.
Start with the 2 whole pies. Each pie has 4 quarters, so 2 × 4 = 8 quarters.
Now include the 3 quarters from the third pie: 8 + 3 = 11 quarters.
[ProductionLabel] DO NOT PRINT — Figure reference: V03a-R7 | The following caption sentence is printable unchanged.
[Caption] 2 whole pies and 3 quarters make 11 quarters.
[ProductionNote] Production note V03a-R7 — Show three identical rectangular pies partitioned into 4 equal parts. First two fully shaded blue, third 3 of 4 parts gold. Arrow from denominator 4 towards whole number 2 indicates multiplication; the next arrow indicates adding numerator 3. Show (2 × 4 + 3)/4 = 11/4. Keep all unit rectangles identical; no piece changes size. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
We have 11 quarter-pieces. Write 11 on top. Keep 4 underneath because each piece is still 1/4 of a pie:
2 3/4 = (2 × 4 + 3)/4 = (8 + 3)/4 = 11/4.
The arrows in the picture show the order: multiply the whole number 2 by the denominator 4; then add the numerator 3. The denominator stays 4.
Now let’s go back from 11/4 to a mixed number. Four quarter-pieces make 1 whole pie. Eight quarter-pieces make 2 whole pies: 2 × 4 = 8.
From our 11 quarter-pieces, we have used 8. There are 11 − 8 = 3 quarter-pieces left. So 11/4 = 2 + 3/4 = 2 3/4.
We can write the division as 11 ÷ 4 = 2 remainder 3. Here, 2 counts the whole pies; the remainder 3 counts the quarter-pieces left.
Check: 2 × 4 + 3 = 11 quarter-pieces again. If we had 12/4, all 12 pieces would make whole pies: 12 ÷ 4 = 3, so 12/4 = 3.
We can now write the same amount as a mixed number or an improper fraction. Let’s use that to compare two amounts.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE015-PANEL01

[PanelizationLabel] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
## Comparing Improper Fractions or Mixed Numbers
Example 1
[Question] Which is smaller, 4/3 or 11/9?
Let’s work it through
[WorkedStep] Let’s find the whole-number parts first. We have already practised this conversion:
[WorkedStep] 4/3: 4 ÷ 3 = 1 remainder 1, so 4/3 = 1 1/3.
[WorkedStep] 11/9: 11 ÷ 9 = 1 remainder 2, so 11/9 = 1 2/9.
[WorkedStep] Both have 1 whole, so compare 1/3 and 2/9. Split each third into 3 equal pieces. The whole now has 3 × 3 = 9 pieces, and our 1/3 has 1 × 3 = 3 of them:
[WorkedStep] 1/3 = (1 × 3)/(3 × 3) = 3/9. The pieces are smaller, but the amount is unchanged.
[WorkedStep] Now 2/9 < 3/9, so 1 2/9 < 1 3/9. The smaller original fraction is 11/9.
[WorkedStep] The shared bottom number, 9, is a common denominator. It makes the pieces the same size, so we can compare how many we have.
[WorkedStep] Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, … . Multiples of 9: 9, 18, 27, … . The first number in both lists is 9. This is the least common multiple (LCM): the smallest positive multiple shared by 3 and 9.
Your turn after Example 1
[Question] Which is smaller, 23/18 or 7/6?
Check your method
[WorkedStep] We can also compare 23/18 and 7/6 directly. Since 6 × 3 = 18, multiply both parts of 7/6 by 3:
[WorkedStep] 7/6 = (7 × 3)/(6 × 3) = 21/18.
[WorkedStep] Since 21/18 < 23/18, the smaller fraction is 7/6.
[WorkedStep] We have compared two fractions. In the next question, we will put three fractions in ascending order. That means smallest first, then the next larger, then the greatest.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE016-PANEL01

[PanelizationLabel] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
Example 2
[Question] Arrange 3/2, 6/5 and 13/10 in ascending order.
Let’s work it through
[WorkedStep] We want the smallest fraction first. Write each fraction as a mixed number:
[WorkedStep] 3/2 = 2/2 + 1/2 = 1 1/2.
[WorkedStep] 6/5 = 5/5 + 1/5 = 1 1/5.
[WorkedStep] 13/10 = 10/10 + 3/10 = 1 3/10.
[WorkedStep] The whole-number part is 1 in all three. Compare the fraction parts: 1/2, 1/5 and 3/10. Use denominator 10, because 2 × 5 = 10 and 5 × 2 = 10.
[WorkedStep] 1/2 = (1 × 5)/(2 × 5) = 5/10.
[WorkedStep] 1/5 = (1 × 2)/(5 × 2) = 2/10. The third fraction, 3/10, already has denominator 10.
[WorkedStep] Compare the fraction parts: 2/10 < 3/10 < 5/10.
[WorkedStep] So 1 2/10 < 1 3/10 < 1 5/10. In the original fractions, the ascending order is 6/5, 13/10, 3/2.
Your turn after Example 2
[Question] Arrange 5/2, 21/10 and 12/5 in ascending order.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] Write each fraction as a mixed number: 5/2 = 2 1/2, 21/10 = 2 1/10, and 12/5 = 2 2/5.
[WorkedStep] All three have a whole-number part of 2. Compare 1/2, 1/10 and 2/5 by using denominator 10:
[WorkedStep] 1/2 = (1 × 5)/(2 × 5) = 5/10; 2/5 = (2 × 2)/(5 × 2) = 4/10.
[WorkedStep] Since 1/10 < 4/10 < 5/10, the mixed numbers are 2 1/10 < 2 4/10 < 2 5/10.
[WorkedStep] Smallest to greatest, in the original fractions: 21/10, 12/5, 5/2.
[WorkedStep] In that question, all the whole-number parts were 2. The next question has different whole-number parts. Check those before comparing the fractions.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE017-PANEL01

Example 3
[Question] Arrange 7/3, 5/4 and 15/8 in ascending order.
Let’s work it through
[WorkedStep] First write each fraction as a mixed number. Divide the top number by the bottom number:
[WorkedStep] 7 ÷ 3 = 2 remainder 1, so 7/3 = 2 1/3.
[WorkedStep] 5 ÷ 4 = 1 remainder 1, so 5/4 = 1 1/4.
[WorkedStep] 15 ÷ 8 = 1 remainder 7, so 15/8 = 1 7/8.
[WorkedStep] The number 2 1/3 is greater than 2. Both 1 1/4 and 1 7/8 are less than 2. So 7/3 is the greatest fraction.
[WorkedStep] Now compare 1 1/4 and 1 7/8. Their whole-number parts are both 1. Change 1/4 to eighths: 1/4 = (1 × 2)/(4 × 2) = 2/8.
[WorkedStep] Since 2/8 < 7/8, we have 1 1/4 < 1 7/8.
[WorkedStep] Ascending order: 5/4, 15/8, 7/3. Check: 1 1/4 < 1 7/8 < 2 1/3.

Your turn after Example 3
[Question] Arrange 19/9, 21/18 and 16/5 in ascending order.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] 19 ÷ 9 = 2 remainder 1, so 19/9 = 2 1/9.
[WorkedStep] 21 ÷ 18 = 1 remainder 3, so 21/18 = 1 3/18.
[WorkedStep] Let’s simplify 3/18: divide both numbers by 3. Then 3/18 = (3 ÷ 3)/(18 ÷ 3) = 1/6. We call this simplifying because we use smaller numbers for the same amount. So 1 3/18 = 1 1/6.
[WorkedStep] 16 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 1, so 16/5 = 3 1/5.
[WorkedStep] The whole-number parts are 2, 1 and 3. Put the number beginning with 1 first, then the number beginning with 2, then the number beginning with 3: 1 1/6 < 2 1/9 < 3 1/5.
[WorkedStep] Ascending order: 21/18, 19/9, 16/5.
Descending order means greatest first, then the next smaller, then the smallest. Let’s use that order in Example 4.

Example 4
[Question] Arrange 7/5, 31/15 and 11/6 in descending order.
Let’s work it through
[WorkedStep] Write the fractions as mixed numbers: 7/5 = 1 2/5, 31/15 = 2 1/15, and 11/6 = 1 5/6.
[WorkedStep] The number 2 1/15 is greater than 2; the other two numbers are less than 2. So 31/15 comes first in descending order.
[WorkedStep] Now compare the fraction parts of 1 2/5 and 1 5/6: 2/5 and 5/6. We need a common denominator for 5 and 6.
[WorkedStep] Multiples of 5: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. The first shared multiple is 30.
[WorkedStep] 2/5 = (2 × 6)/(5 × 6) = 12/30.
[WorkedStep] 5/6 = (5 × 5)/(6 × 5) = 25/30.
[WorkedStep] Since 25/30 > 12/30, we have 1 5/6 > 1 2/5. So 11/6 comes before 7/5.
[WorkedStep] Descending order: 31/15, 11/6, 7/5.
Your turn after Example 4
[Question] Arrange 17/9, 23/10 and 14/5 in descending order.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] 17/9 = 1 8/9; 23/10 = 2 3/10; 14/5 = 2 4/5.
[WorkedStep] Compare 2 3/10 and 2 4/5. Change 4/5 to tenths: 4/5 = (4 × 2)/(5 × 2) = 8/10.
[WorkedStep] Since 8/10 > 3/10, the order is 2 8/10 > 2 3/10 > 1 8/9.
[WorkedStep] Descending order in the original fractions: 14/5, 23/10, 17/9.

## Practice 2A
Try each question before checking its solution. When a question asks you to explain, give your reason as well as your answer.
We used the direct method after Example 1: 7/6 = (7 × 3)/(6 × 3) = 21/18. Let’s use the same idea below: make the denominators match, then compare the top numbers.
Practice 2A Question 1
[Question] Circle the greater fraction in each pair.
[Question] (a)  11/7, 33/28
[Question] (b)  11/9, 29/18
[Question] (c)  27/10, 37/15
[Question] (d)  9/2, 14/3
[Question] (e)  19/10, 15/8
[Question] (f)  19/12, 31/15
Check your method

Practice 2A Question 4
[Question] Nurul thinks of a number x such that 5 2/3 < x < 5 8/9. Write one possible value of x.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] The letter x stands for the number we must find. We need a number greater than 5 2/3 and smaller than 5 8/9. The sign < means “is less than”.
[WorkedStep] Both given numbers have whole-number part 5. First give their fraction parts, 2/3 and 8/9, the same denominator.
[WorkedStep] 2/3 = (2 × 3)/(3 × 3) = 6/9. The fraction 8/9 already has denominator 9.
[WorkedStep] So we need 5 6/9 < x < 5 8/9.
[WorkedStep] The fraction 7/9 lies between 6/9 and 8/9. One possible answer is x = 5 7/9.
[WorkedStep] Check: 5 6/9 < 5 7/9 < 5 8/9.
[WorkedStep] We cannot choose x = 5 2/3 or x = 5 8/9. The question asks for a number between them, not a number equal to either of them.

Practice 2A Question 5
[Question] Jake thinks of a number x such that 2 1/5 < x < 2 1/4. Write one possible value of x.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] We need a number between 2 1/5 and 2 1/4. Both whole-number parts are 2, so compare 1/5 and 1/4. Give them denominator 20:
[WorkedStep] 1/5 = (1 × 4)/(5 × 4) = 4/20; 1/4 = (1 × 5)/(4 × 5) = 5/20.
[WorkedStep] We need a fraction between 4/20 and 5/20. There is no whole number between the top numbers 4 and 5. Let’s split each twentieth into 2 equal pieces so that we can use smaller parts:
[WorkedStep] 4/20 = (4 × 2)/(20 × 2) = 8/40; 5/20 = (5 × 2)/(20 × 2) = 10/40.
[WorkedStep] Now we have room for 9/40: 8/40 < 9/40 < 10/40.
[WorkedStep] Put the whole-number part 2 back. One possible answer is x = 2 9/40.
[WorkedStep] Check: 2 8/40 < 2 9/40 < 2 10/40.

Practice 2A Question 6
[Question] Kylian has 21/10, 21/11 and 32/15. Arrange them from smallest to greatest.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] 21/11 = 1 10/11 is less than 2. The others are 21/10 = 2 1/10 and 32/15 = 2 2/15.
[WorkedStep] Compare the fraction parts of 2 1/10 and 2 2/15: 1/10 = (1 × 3)/(10 × 3) = 3/30, and 2/15 = (2 × 2)/(15 × 2) = 4/30. Since 3/30 < 4/30, we have 2 1/10 < 2 2/15.
[WorkedStep] Smallest to greatest: 21/11, 21/10, 32/15.
Practice 2A Question 7
[Question] Nellie has 14/11, 5/2 and 33/22. Arrange them from greatest to smallest.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] 5/2 = 2 1/2, while 14/11 = 1 3/11 and 33/22 = 1 11/22. So 5/2 is greatest. For the other two, 3/11 = (3 × 2)/(11 × 2) = 6/22 < 11/22.
[WorkedStep] Greatest to smallest: 5/2, 33/22, 14/11.
Practice 2A Question 8
[Question] Raju needs a fraction for the box: 11/7 < □ < 12/7. What could it be? Explain how you found it.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] We need a fraction greater than 11/7 and smaller than 12/7. No whole number fits between 11 and 12, so we cannot keep denominator 7 and use a whole-number numerator.
[WorkedStep] Make the parts smaller by giving both fractions denominator 14:
[WorkedStep] 11/7 = (11 × 2)/(7 × 2) = 22/14; 12/7 = (12 × 2)/(7 × 2) = 24/14.
[WorkedStep] The number 23 fits between 22 and 24. One possible answer is 23/14, because 22/14 < 23/14 < 24/14.

Practice 2A Question 9
[Question] Arrange 3/2, 4/3, 5/4 and 6/5 in ascending order. What do you observe?
Check your method
[WorkedStep] Write each fraction as a mixed number: 3/2 = 1 1/2, 4/3 = 1 1/3, 5/4 = 1 1/4, and 6/5 = 1 1/5.
[WorkedStep] Each whole-number part is 1, so compare 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 and 1/5. The next picture uses equal-sized rectangles for 1 whole. Each row shades 1 part.
[ProductionLabel] DO NOT PRINT — Figure reference: V05a-R7 | The following caption sentence is printable unchanged.
[Caption] More equal parts in the same whole make each part smaller.
[ProductionNote] Production note V05a-R7 — Four identical-width bars partitioned into 2,3,4,5 equal pieces; shade exactly one in each. Explicitly identify each reference bar as the same whole. Label 1/2,1/3,1/4,1/5 and the ascending comparison. Do not vary whole widths. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
[WorkedStep] One of 5 equal parts is smaller than one of 4 equal parts, and so on: 1/5 < 1/4 < 1/3 < 1/2.
[WorkedStep] Add the whole-number part 1 to each: 1 1/5 < 1 1/4 < 1 1/3 < 1 1/2.
[WorkedStep] Ascending order in the original fractions: 6/5, 5/4, 4/3, 3/2.
[WorkedStep] Notice the pattern: 3/2, 4/3, 5/4, 6/5 each have 1 more on top than underneath. Each is 1 plus a smaller fraction: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, then 1/5. That is why these four numbers get smaller. Adding 1 to both parts of a fraction does not always make it smaller.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE024-PANEL01

[ProductionNote] Dispenser control reference: the supply tap isolates the brass tank from the measuring cup. The cup’s adjustable stop sets its fill capacity, calibrated in batter mass for this recipe. The long cool-side handle operates the cup outlet; a mechanical interlock closes the tank feed before opening that outlet. At rest the outlet is closed; the supply tap may charge the cup. Lowering the handle isolates the tank and releases only the cup contents. The heater is independent. Use these same three controls in every view. The original stock tray and the separate wrap-filling vessels remain distinct.

[ProductionLabel] Production instructions are non-printing. Exact reader text is assigned beneath each visual beat.
[ProductionNote] Setting. Location CH02 L02: The pale physical-left recipe counter has a cupboard beneath, a dry book-and-balance work area (equipment remains in the cupboard until Visual beat CH02 01G A), a brass batter tank and adjustable measuring cup behind the cool working edge, a separate cooking plate behind the guard and a dry shelf for finished plates. The cooking plate is behind the counter. Ahana’s lamp rests on the near packing bench; her sketchbook is packed. Tara’s evidence sleeve is secured in her sash pocket. No character reaches over the hot plate. The two cooled wrap-filling bowls hold 1¾ kg and 2½ kg. They are separate from the measured batter tray. The mixing bowl is empty. Dosa supply closed; portion stop uncorrected.

# 2.2 Addition of Mixed Numbers
So far, we have compared fractions. Now let’s add them. Start with 1/6 + 2/6.
Each full rectangle in the next picture represents 1 whole, cut into 6 equal parts. One blue part shows 1/6. Two gold parts show 2/6.
Put the coloured parts together. We have 1 + 2 = 3 parts, and each part is still one sixth, 1/6, of the whole. So the total is 3/6.
[ProductionLabel] DO NOT PRINT — Figure reference: V06a-R | The following caption sentence is printable unchanged.
[Caption] Count equal pieces to get 3/6.
[ProductionNote] Production note V06a-R — Two starting bars each represent the same whole and show 1/6 and 2/6. The second state uses exactly 6 equal parts and shows 1 + 2 pieces. Blue is the first amount, gold added pieces; red crosses indicate removed pieces. Result 3/6. Every reference whole has identical width in both stages. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
1/6 + 2/6 = (1 + 2)/6 = 3/6. Three of six equal pieces cover half the whole. In symbols, 3/6 = (3 ÷ 3)/(6 ÷ 3) = 1/2.

What about 7/10 + 1/5? The denominators 10 and 5 are different. Let’s give both fractions denominator 10 before adding.
Each full rectangle in the next picture is 1 whole. Split each fifth into 2 equal parts. That makes 5 × 2 = 10 parts in the whole, and the shaded fifth becomes 1 × 2 = 2 tenths:
1/5 = (1 × 2)/(5 × 2) = 2/10.

Now let’s add 3 1/6 and 2 1/6. We have two jobs: add the whole-number parts, then add the fraction parts.
Example 5
[Question] Evaluate each sum.
[Question] (a)  3 1/6 + 2 1/6
[Question] (b)  2 1/8 + 1 7/8
Let’s work it through
[WorkedStep] (a) Start with 3 1/6 + 2 1/6. Keep the whole numbers and fractions separate for a moment.
[WorkedStep] First add the whole-number parts: 3 + 2 = 5.
[WorkedStep] Next add the fraction parts: 1/6 + 1/6 = (1 + 1)/6 = 2/6.
[WorkedStep] Put those results together: 3 1/6 + 2 1/6 = 5 2/6.
[WorkedStep] Now simplify the fraction part, 2/6. Divide its top and bottom by 2: 2/6 = (2 ÷ 2)/(6 ÷ 2) = 1/3.
[WorkedStep] So our answer is 5 2/6 = 5 1/3.
[WorkedStep] Our total, 5 1/3, is a little more than 3 + 2 = 5, as we expected.
[WorkedStep] (b) Now add 2 1/8 + 1 7/8. Add the whole-number parts: 2 + 1 = 3. Add the fraction parts: 1/8 + 7/8 = 8/8 = 1.
[WorkedStep] The fraction parts have made 1 extra whole: 8/8 = 1. Add that to the 3 wholes.
[WorkedStep] 2 1/8 + 1 7/8 = 3 + 8/8 = 3 + 1 = 4.
[WorkedStep] Check with a nearby estimate: 2 1/8 is near 2 and 1 7/8 is near 2, so a total of 4 makes sense.
Your turn after Example 5
[Question] Evaluate and simplify.
[Question] (a)  4 3/7 + 2 2/7
[Question] (b)  4 3/5 + 1 4/5
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) 4 3/7 + 2 2/7 = (4 + 2) + (3 + 2)/7 = 6 5/7.
[WorkedStep] (b) 4 3/5 + 1 4/5 = 5 + 7/5.
[WorkedStep] Here 7/5 = 5/5 + 2/5 = 1 2/5, so the total is 5 + 1 2/5 = 6 2/5.

[WorkedStep] In those additions, the two fraction parts already had the same denominator. Next we will add numbers such as 2 1/3 and 1 1/6, where the denominators 3 and 6 are different.
Example 6
[Question] Evaluate each sum.
[Question] (a)  2 1/3 + 1 1/6
[Question] (b)  3 1/5 + 1 3/10
Let’s work it through
[WorkedStep] (a) We are adding 2 1/3 + 1 1/6. For a quick estimate, use 2 instead of 2 1/3 and 1 instead of 1 1/6: 2 + 1 = 3. The exact answer will be a little higher.
[WorkedStep] Add the whole-number parts: 2 + 1 = 3.
[WorkedStep] Next add 1/3 and 1/6. Their denominators differ, so make them match:
[WorkedStep] 1/3 = (1 × 2)/(3 × 2) = 2/6. Keep the other fraction, 1/6, unchanged.
[WorkedStep] Add the fractions: 2/6 + 1/6 = 3/6. Together with the 3 wholes, that gives 3 3/6.
[WorkedStep] Simplify: 3/6 = (3 ÷ 3)/(6 ÷ 3) = 1/2.
[WorkedStep] Answer: 3 1/2. Check: 3 1/2 is 1/2 more than our estimate of 3.
[WorkedStep] (b) For 3 1/5 + 1 3/10, an estimate using nearby halves is 3 + 1 1/2 = 4 1/2.
[WorkedStep] For the exact sum, add the whole-number parts: 3 + 1 = 4. Then give the fraction parts, 1/5 and 3/10, denominator 10:
[WorkedStep] 1/5 = (1 × 2)/(5 × 2) = 2/10. The fraction 3/10 stays as it is.
[WorkedStep] Add: 2/10 + 3/10 = 5/10. Simplify: 5/10 = (5 ÷ 5)/(10 ÷ 5) = 1/2.
[WorkedStep] So 3 1/5 + 1 3/10 = 4 + 1/2 = 4 1/2. Our estimate, 4 1/2, happens to equal the exact answer this time.

Next we will add 3 1/3 + 1 3/4. The fraction parts have denominators 3 and 4. Neither 3 nor 4 works as a common denominator, so we will find a new denominator for both fractions.
Example 7
[Question] Evaluate each sum.
[Question] (a)  3 1/3 + 1 3/4
[Question] (b)  4 1/5 + 1 1/3
Let’s work it through
[WorkedStep] (a) First estimate using nearby halves: 3 1/3 is near 3 1/2, and 1 3/4 is near 1 1/2. So a useful estimate is 3 1/2 + 1 1/2 = 5.
[WorkedStep] Now add the whole-number parts exactly: 3 + 1 = 4.
[WorkedStep] For the fraction parts, 1/3 and 3/4, find a common denominator. Multiples of 3 are 3, 6, 9, 12, … . Multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, … . The first shared multiple is 12.
[WorkedStep] Give 1/3 denominator 12: 1/3 = (1 × 4)/(3 × 4) = 4/12.
[WorkedStep] Give 3/4 denominator 12 too: 3/4 = (3 × 3)/(4 × 3) = 9/12.
[WorkedStep] Add the fraction parts: 4/12 + 9/12 = 13/12.
[WorkedStep] We can take 1 whole out of 13/12: 13/12 = 12/12 + 1/12 = 1 + 1/12.
[WorkedStep] Add the extra whole to the 4 we already had: 4 + 1 + 1/12 = 5 1/12.
[WorkedStep] Our answer, 5 1/12, is close to the estimate of 5.

## Practice 2B
An estimate uses easy numbers near the given numbers. For example, 4 2/3 is near 5 and 2 1/3 is near 2, so their sum is about 5 + 2 = 7. Then calculate the exact answer. Different sensible estimates are possible.
Practice 2B Question 1
[Question] Evaluate. Give answers in simplest form.
[Question] (a)  2 1/4 + 1/4
[Question] (b)  3 5/8 + 2 7/8
[Question] (c)  1 6/19 + 2 13/19
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) 2 1/4 + 1/4 = 2 + (1 + 1)/4 = 2 2/4 = 2 1/2.
[WorkedStep] (b) 3 5/8 + 2 7/8 = 5 + (5 + 7)/8 = 5 + 12/8.
[WorkedStep] Regroup 12/8 = 1 4/8 = 1 1/2, so the total is 5 + 1 1/2 = 6 1/2.
[WorkedStep] (c) 1 6/19 + 2 13/19 = 3 + (6 + 13)/19 = 3 + 1 = 4.
Practice 2B Question 2
[Question] Estimate first, then find the actual value. Give answers in simplest form.
[Question] (a)  4 2/3 + 2 1/3
[Question] (b)  3 1/4 + 1 3/4
[Question] (c)  6 1/6 + 2 5/6
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) Estimate: 5 + 2 = 7.
[WorkedStep] Actual value: 4 2/3 + 2 1/3 = 6 + (2 + 1)/3 = 6 + 1 = 7.
[WorkedStep] (b) Estimate: 3 + 2 = 5.
[WorkedStep] Actual value: 3 1/4 + 1 3/4 = 4 + (1 + 3)/4 = 4 + 1 = 5.
[WorkedStep] (c) Estimate: 6 + 3 = 9.
[WorkedStep] Actual value: 6 1/6 + 2 5/6 = 8 + (1 + 5)/6 = 8 + 1 = 9.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE034-PANEL01

Practice 2B Question 3
[Question] Evaluate. Give answers in simplest form.
[Question] (a)  2 3/5 + 1 3/10
[Question] (b)  3 7/10 + 1 1/2
[Question] (c)  2 1/3 + 3 5/9
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) 3/5 = (3 × 2)/(5 × 2) = 6/10.
[WorkedStep] 2 3/5 + 1 3/10 = 3 + (6 + 3)/10 = 3 9/10.
[WorkedStep] (b) 1/2 = (1 × 5)/(2 × 5) = 5/10.
[WorkedStep] 3 7/10 + 1 1/2 = 4 + (7 + 5)/10 = 4 + 12/10.
[WorkedStep] Since 12/10 = 1 2/10 = 1 1/5, the total is 5 1/5.
[WorkedStep] (c) 1/3 = (1 × 3)/(3 × 3) = 3/9.
[WorkedStep] 2 1/3 + 3 5/9 = 5 + (3 + 5)/9 = 5 8/9.
Practice 2B Question 4
[Question] Estimate first, then find the actual value. Give answers in simplest form.
[Question] (a)  3 1/2 + 1 2/3
[Question] (b)  10 5/7 + 8 5/14
[Question] (c)  9 5/9 + 7 1/3
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  Estimate: 3 + 2 = 5.
[WorkedStep] Use denominator 6: 1/2 = (1 × 3)/(2 × 3) = 3/6; 2/3 = (2 × 2)/(3 × 2) = 4/6.
[WorkedStep] 3 1/2 + 1 2/3 = 4 + 3/6 + 4/6 = 4 + 7/6.
[WorkedStep] Regroup 7/6 = 1 1/6, giving 4 + 1 1/6 = 5 1/6.
[WorkedStep] (b)  Estimate: 11 + 8 = 19.
[WorkedStep] Change 5/7 to (5 × 2)/(7 × 2) = 10/14.
[WorkedStep] 10 5/7 + 8 5/14 = 18 + 10/14 + 5/14 = 18 + 15/14.
[WorkedStep] Regroup 15/14 = 1 1/14, giving 18 + 1 1/14 = 19 1/14.
[WorkedStep] (c)  Estimate: 10 + 7 = 17.
[WorkedStep] Change 1/3 to (1 × 3)/(3 × 3) = 3/9.
[WorkedStep] 9 5/9 + 7 1/3 = 16 + (5 + 3)/9 = 16 8/9.

[PanelizationLabel] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
Practice 2B Question 5
[Question] Read each method. Comment on it and improve the answer.
[Question] (a)  James writes: 1 2/3 + 2 5/6 = 5/3 + 17/6 = 10/6 + 17/6 = 27/6.
[Question] (b)  Serene writes: 1 2/3 + 2 5/6 = 1 4/6 + 2 5/6 = 3 9/6 = 3 3/2.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) James’s method is correct. He changes both mixed numbers to improper fractions: 1 2/3 = (1 × 3 + 2)/3 = 5/3, and 2 5/6 = (2 × 6 + 5)/6 = 17/6.
[WorkedStep] He then uses 5/3 = (5 × 2)/(3 × 2) = 10/6 and adds 10/6 + 17/6 = 27/6.
[WorkedStep] His answer can be simplified: 27/6 = (27 ÷ 3)/(6 ÷ 3) = 9/2 = 4 1/2.
[WorkedStep] (b) Serene’s calculation gives the right amount too. But in her answer, 3 3/2, the fraction part 3/2 is larger than 1. A mixed number should have a fraction part smaller than 1.
[WorkedStep] Change 3/2 to 1 1/2, then add: 3 + 1 1/2 = 4 1/2.
[WorkedStep] Both methods give 4 1/2.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE036-PANEL01

# 2.3 Multiplication and Division of Proper Fractions
What does 1/3 × 5 mean? It means 5 lots of 1/3.
In this picture, each small blue rectangle is 1/3 of a whole bar. Count 5 of them. Three pieces fill 1 whole bar; 2 pieces remain. So we have 1 whole and 2/3 of another whole.
[ProductionLabel] DO NOT PRINT — Figure reference: V10 | The following caption sentence is printable unchanged.
[Caption] Five one-third pieces regroup into one whole and two thirds.
[ProductionNote] Production note V10 — Show five identical one-third pieces, then regroup the same pieces as 1 2/3 within outlines of equal wholes. Three pieces fill one whole. No piece changes area. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
1/3 × 5 = 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 + 1/3 = 5/3 = 1 2/3.
Now we will find 1/5 of 1/3. This means taking only one fifth of the shaded third, rather than taking 5 copies of it. Let’s show the difference with a picture.

## Multiplying a Fraction by a Fraction
In Stage 1, the full square represents 1 whole sheet of paper.
In Stage 2, divide the sheet into 3 equal strips. Shade 1 strip blue: that is 1/3 of the sheet.
In Stage 3, divide the blue strip into 5 equal pieces and choose 1 of them. The dark, hatched piece is 1/5 of the blue 1/3. Extend the same cuts through the rest of the square so we can count the equal pieces in the whole sheet.
[ProductionLabel] DO NOT PRINT — Figure reference: V11a-R | The following caption sentence is printable unchanged.
[Caption] Take 1/5 of the shaded 1/3: 1 of the 15 equal cells.
[ProductionNote] Production note V11a-R — Three identical squares. Stage1 whole uncut; stage2 three equal horizontal rows, 1 blue; stage3 five equal columns crossing all three rows, 15 equal cells. Select first-column cells in the 1 blue rows using dark teal and hatching. Exactly 1 selected cells; product 1/15. No other value or later example shown. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
Count the whole sheet: 3 rows × 5 columns = 15 equal pieces. We chose 1 dark piece, so the answer is 1/15 of the sheet.
We write “of” as multiplication here: 1/3 × 1/5 = (1 × 1)/(3 × 5) = 1/15.
The diagram explains the calculation. Multiplying the denominators, 3 × 5, gives the 15 equal parts in the whole. Multiplying the numerators, 1 × 1, gives the 1 part chosen.
So, to multiply fractions, multiply top by top and bottom by bottom, then simplify. The next example shows this with 2/3 × 1/5.
Notice that 1/15 is smaller than 1/3. Taking only 1/5 of a positive amount makes it smaller. Multiplication does not always make a number bigger!

Example 8
[Question] Evaluate and simplify.
[Question] (a)  2/3 × 1/5
[Question] (b)  6/11 × 22/30
Let’s work it through
[WorkedStep] (a) We need 1/5 of 2/3. Again, the full square is 1 whole sheet. Shade 2 of its 3 equal strips blue: that is 2/3.
[WorkedStep] Divide each blue strip into 5 equal pieces. Take 1 piece from each strip. We take 1 × 2 = 2 small pieces altogether; these are the dark, hatched pieces in the picture.
[ProductionLabel] DO NOT PRINT — Figure reference: V11b-R | The following caption sentence is printable unchanged.
[Caption] Take 1/5 of the shaded 2/3: 2 of the 15 equal cells.
[ProductionNote] Production note V11b-R — Three identical squares. Stage1 whole uncut; stage2 three equal horizontal rows, 2 blue; stage3 five equal columns crossing all three rows, 15 equal cells. Select first-column cells in the 2 blue rows using dark teal and hatching. Exactly 2 selected cells; product 2/15. No other value or later example shown. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
[WorkedStep] The whole sheet contains 3 × 5 = 15 equal pieces. The 2 dark pieces therefore make 2/15 of the sheet:
[WorkedStep] 2/3 × 1/5 = (2 × 1)/(3 × 5) = 2/15.
[WorkedStep] Check: 2/3 = 10/15, and 1/5 = 3/15. Our answer, 2/15, is smaller than both 10/15 and 3/15.

[WorkedStep] (b) Now calculate 6/11 × 22/30. Multiplying directly gives (6 × 22)/(11 × 30) = 132/330. There is a way to keep the numbers smaller: simplify before multiplying.
[WorkedStep] Write the multiplication as one fraction: (6 × 22)/(11 × 30).
[WorkedStep] Divide the top factor 6 and the bottom factor 30 by 6: 6 ÷ 6 = 1 and 30 ÷ 6 = 5. The other factors, 22 and 11, stay unchanged:
[WorkedStep] (6 × 22)/(11 × 30) = (1 × 22)/(11 × 5).
[WorkedStep] Now divide the top factor 22 and the bottom factor 11 by 11: 22 ÷ 11 = 2 and 11 ÷ 11 = 1:
[WorkedStep] (1 × 22)/(11 × 5) = (1 × 2)/(1 × 5) = 2/5.
[WorkedStep] This is called cancellation. We divided the numerator and denominator by the same number, so the fraction kept the same value. Each cancelled number was a factor, meaning a number being multiplied. This method does not let us cross out numbers that are being added.
[WorkedStep] We can also simplify 22/30 first: 22/30 = (22 ÷ 2)/(30 ÷ 2) = 11/15. Then 6/11 × 11/15 = (6 × 1)/(1 × 15) = 6/15 = (6 ÷ 3)/(15 ÷ 3) = 2/5.
Your turn after Example 8
[Question] Evaluate and simplify.
[Question] (a)  2/7 × 5/9
[Question] (b)  12/39 × 13/60
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) Multiply top by top and bottom by bottom: 2/7 × 5/9 = (2 × 5)/(7 × 9) = 10/63.
[WorkedStep] (b) Write 12/39 × 13/60 as (12 × 13)/(39 × 60).
[WorkedStep] Divide 12 and 60 by 12, and 13 and 39 by 13. That leaves 1 and 1 on top, with 3 and 5 underneath:
[WorkedStep] So (12 × 13)/(39 × 60) = (1 × 13)/(39 × 5) = (1 × 1)/(3 × 5) = 1/15.

[PanelizationLabel] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
[PrintField] FRIENDLY TEACHER BRIDGE — PRINT ONLY THIS
[TeacherBridge] Four plates are waiting. Let’s see how division counts servings, starting with apples before we return to the batter.
[PrintField] TEACHING COPY BEGINS — ALL SUPPLIED LEARNER CONTENT FOLLOWS; PRODUCTION NOTES REMAIN NON-PRINTING
For division, ask how many groups we can make. Suppose we have 6 apples and put 2 apples in each group. Then 6 ÷ 2 = 3 groups.
Now let each serving be 1/2 of an apple. Each apple gives 2 servings, so 6 apples give 6 × 2 = 12 servings. We write 6 ÷ 1/2 = 12.
Each row in the next diagram represents the same 6 apples. A length of 1 stands for 1 apple. The colours mark the groups: 2 apples per group in the first row, 1/2 apple per group in the second row. We will use the third row next.
[ProductionLabel] DO NOT PRINT — Figure reference: V12 | The following caption sentence is printable unchanged.
[Caption] Divide 6 apples into groups of 2, 1/2 or 2/3 apple.
[ProductionNote] Production note V12 — Three rows use the same total of six wholes: groups of 2 give 3; groups of 1/2 give 12; groups of 2/3 give 9. Draw exact partitions and braces, with no lost pieces. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
Now look at the third row: each serving is 2/3 of an apple. Cut every apple into 3 equal parts. From 6 apples we get 6 × 3 = 18 one-third pieces.
Each serving needs 2 of those pieces, so 18 ÷ 2 = 9 servings.
6 ÷ 2/3 = (6 × 3) ÷ 2 = 18 ÷ 2 = 9.
The calculation multiplied by 3, then divided by 2. We can write those two operations as multiplying by 3/2:
6 × 3/2 = (6 × 3)/2 = 18/2 = 9.
The fraction 3/2 is called the reciprocal of 2/3. To find it, swap the top and bottom numbers: 2 over 3 becomes 3 over 2.
Check: 2/3 × 3/2 = (2 × 3)/(3 × 2) = 6/6 = 1. Any non-zero number multiplied by its reciprocal gives 1. Zero has no reciprocal.
So 6 ÷ 2/3 = 6 × 3/2. The starting number, 6, stays unchanged. Only the fraction we divide by, 2/3, is turned over. Let’s use the same idea when the starting amount is a fraction.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE046-PANEL01

[PanelizationLabel] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
## Dividing a Fraction by a Fraction
A division can also give us less than 1 group. For example, we may have less material than one full group needs. The answer will then tell us what fraction of a group we can make.
Example 9
[Question] Evaluate and simplify.
[Question] (a)  3/8 ÷ 4/5
[Question] (b)  1/9 ÷ 2/3
[Question] (c)  5/11 ÷ 10/11
Let’s work it through
[WorkedStep] (a) We need 3/8 ÷ 4/5. Think of a ribbon 1 metre long. We have 3/8 metre, and one full group needs 4/5 metre. How much of that group can we make?
[WorkedStep] In the diagram, each full bar stands for 1 metre. To compare the lengths, write 3/8 and 4/5 with denominator 40: 8 × 5 = 40, and 5 × 8 = 40.
[WorkedStep] 3/8 = (3 × 5)/(8 × 5) = 15/40.
[WorkedStep] 4/5 = (4 × 8)/(5 × 8) = 32/40.
[ProductionLabel] DO NOT PRINT — Figure reference: V13-R | The following caption sentence is printable unchanged.
[Caption] We have 15 pieces; 1 group needs 32 of those pieces.
[ProductionNote] Production note V13-R — Two equal-width bars each represent 1 metre of ribbon, partitioned into exactly 40 equal cells. Shade 15 cells blue and 32 cells gold. Label available length 15/40 m and length for 1 group 32/40 m. Brace only the 32-cell portion as 1 group. Distinguish 1/40 metre from 1/32 of a group. The quotient 15/32 counts groups. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
[WorkedStep] The blue length has 15 small pieces. One full gold length needs 32 pieces of that same size.
[WorkedStep] We have 15 of the 32 pieces needed. So we have 15/32 of one gold length. That is why the answer is 15/32.
[WorkedStep] The shorter calculation gives the same answer. Keep 3/8 and multiply by the reciprocal of 4/5, which is 5/4:
[WorkedStep] 3/8 ÷ 4/5 = 3/8 × 5/4 = (3 × 5)/(8 × 4) = 15/32.
[WorkedStep] Check the length: 15/32 × 4/5 = 60/160 = 3/8 metre, the amount we started with.

[PanelizationLabel] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
Let’s compare three divisions with the same starting number, 6.
6 ÷ 1/2 = 12. Dividing by 1/2, a positive fraction below 1, gives a number greater than 6.
6 ÷ 3/2 = 6 × 2/3 = 4. Dividing by 3/2, a fraction greater than 1, gives a number smaller than 6.
6 ÷ 2/2 = 6 ÷ 1 = 6. Dividing by 1 leaves the number unchanged.
These size checks apply to positive starting amounts. Read the fraction you divide by before deciding whether the answer should be bigger or smaller.
Our answer 15/32 in Example 9 was part of a group. But if a question asks how many full bottles we can fill, a part-filled bottle does not count as full. Watch for that word in the next question.

[PanelizationLabel] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
Example 10
[Question] Rina has 9/10 L of cooking oil. She pours it into bottles holding 1/6 L each. How many full bottles can she fill?
Let’s work it through
[WorkedStep] We have 9/10 L of oil. Each bottle holds 1/6 L. Divide the total oil by the amount for one bottle:
[WorkedStep] Number of bottlefuls = 9/10 ÷ 1/6.
[WorkedStep] 9/10 ÷ 1/6 = 9/10 × 6/1 = 54/10 = (54 ÷ 2)/(10 ÷ 2) = 27/5.
[WorkedStep] Change 27/5 to a mixed number: 27 ÷ 5 = 5 remainder 2, so 27/5 = 5 2/5.
[WorkedStep] This means 5 full bottles and 2/5 of another bottle. The question asks for full bottles, so the answer is 5.
[WorkedStep] Let’s check the oil left. Five bottles use 5 × 1/6 = 5/6 L. Compare that with the 9/10 L available, using denominator 30:
[WorkedStep] 5/6 = (5 × 5)/(6 × 5) = 25/30 L; 9/10 = (9 × 3)/(10 × 3) = 27/30 L.
[WorkedStep] Oil left: 27/30 − 25/30 = 2/30 = 1/15 L. Six full bottles would need 6 × 1/6 = 1 L, more than our 9/10 L. So we must stop at 5 full bottles.
[WorkedStep] In the picture, each rectangle is 1 bottle holding 1/6 L. Five are full. The sixth is 2/5 full. Here 2/5 describes a fraction of a bottle; the actual oil left is 1/15 L, not 2/5 L.
[ProductionLabel] DO NOT PRINT — Figure reference: V14 | The following caption sentence is printable unchanged.
[Caption] The leftover oil fills only part of the next bottle.

Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
Your turn after Example 10

Check your method

## Practice 2C
Practice 2C Question 1
[Question] Multiply and give answers in simplest form.
[Question] (a)  1/3 × 6/7
[Question] (b)  2/7 × 6/7
[Question] (c)  3/5 × 7/8
[Question] (d)  3/4 × 7/12
[Question] (e)  2/13 × 26/39
[Question] (f)  5/11 × 55/77
[Question] (g)  2/3 × 6/14
[Question] (h)  2/9 × 3/10
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) Let’s keep the numbers small: divide 6 and 3 by 3 before multiplying. 1/3 × 6/7 = (1 × (6 ÷ 3))/((3 ÷ 3) × 7).
[WorkedStep] = (1 × 2)/(1 × 7) = 2/7.
[WorkedStep] (b)  2/7 × 6/7 = (2 × 6)/(7 × 7) = 12/49.
[WorkedStep] (c)  3/5 × 7/8 = (3 × 7)/(5 × 8) = 21/40.
[WorkedStep] (d) 3/4 × 7/12 = ((3 ÷ 3) × 7)/(4 × (12 ÷ 3)) = (1 × 7)/(4 × 4) = 7/16.
[WorkedStep] (e) 2/13 × 26/39 = (2 × (26 ÷ 13))/((13 ÷ 13) × 39).
[WorkedStep] = (2 × 2)/(1 × 39) = 4/39.
[WorkedStep] (f) 5/11 × 55/77 = (5 × (55 ÷ 11))/((11 ÷ 11) × 77).
[WorkedStep] = (5 × 5)/(1 × 77) = 25/77.
[WorkedStep] (g) Divide 6 and 3 by 3, then 2 and 14 by 2: 2/3 × 6/14 = (2 × 2)/(1 × 14) = (1 × 2)/(1 × 7) = 2/7.
[WorkedStep] (h) Divide 2 and 10 by 2, and 3 and 9 by 3: 2/9 × 3/10 = (1 × 1)/(3 × 5) = 1/15.

Practice 2C Question 2
[Question] Evaluate and give answers in simplest form.
[Question] (a)  1/2 ÷ 1/3
[Question] (b)  4/5 ÷ 2/3
[Question] (c)  3/5 ÷ 4/5
[Question] (d)  4/9 ÷ 5/3
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) 1/2 ÷ 1/3 = 1/2 × 3/1 = 3/2 = 1 1/2.
[WorkedStep] (b) 4/5 ÷ 2/3 = 4/5 × 3/2 = ((4 ÷ 2) × 3)/(5 × (2 ÷ 2)) = 6/5 = 1 1/5.
[WorkedStep] (c) 3/5 ÷ 4/5 = 3/5 × 5/4 = (3 × (5 ÷ 5))/((5 ÷ 5) × 4) = 3/4.
[WorkedStep] (d) Dividing by 5/3, which is greater than 1, should make 4/9 smaller. 4/9 ÷ 5/3 = 4/9 × 3/5.
[WorkedStep] = (4 × (3 ÷ 3))/((9 ÷ 3) × 5) = 4/15.

Practice 2C Question 3
[Question] Evaluate and give answers in simplest form.
[Question] (a)  3/7 × 2/3 + 4/7
[Question] (b)  4/5 − 2/3 ÷ 4/8
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) The calculation is 3/7 × 2/3 + 4/7. Do multiplication before addition:
[WorkedStep] 3/7 × 2/3 = ((3 ÷ 3) × 2)/(7 × (3 ÷ 3)) = 2/7.
[WorkedStep] Now add: 2/7 + 4/7 = (2 + 4)/7 = 6/7.
[WorkedStep] (b) The calculation is 4/5 − 2/3 ÷ 4/8. Do division before subtraction:
[WorkedStep] 2/3 ÷ 4/8 = 2/3 × 8/4 = (2 × (8 ÷ 4))/(3 × (4 ÷ 4)) = 4/3.
[WorkedStep] Now calculate 4/5 − 4/3. Give both fractions denominator 15:
[WorkedStep] 4/5 = (4 × 3)/(5 × 3) = 12/15; 4/3 = (4 × 5)/(3 × 5) = 20/15.
[WorkedStep] We now have 12/15 − 20/15. Taking away 12/15 gets us to 0. There is still 8/15 to take away, so the answer goes below 0.
[WorkedStep] 12/15 − 20/15 = (12 - 20)/15 = −8/15.
[WorkedStep] The minus sign in −8/15 means the answer is 8/15 below zero. Check: −8/15 + 20/15 = 12/15.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE052-PANEL01

Practice 2C Question 4
[Question] Sarah claims that 2/5 × 3/8 = 6/4. Without calculating the product, explain whether she is correct.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] Sarah is not correct. In 2/5 × 3/8, we take only 3/8 of 2/5. Since 3/8 is less than 1, the answer must be smaller than 2/5.
[WorkedStep] But her answer, 6/4, is greater than 1 because 6 > 4. The starting amount, 2/5, is less than 1 because 2 < 5. Her answer is too large. We have checked this without calculating the product.
Practice 2C Question 5
[Question] Ali claims that 6/7 ÷ 3/5 = 2/15. Without calculating, explain whether he is correct. If he is wrong, correct his answer.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] Ali is not correct. Dividing 6/7 by 3/5, a positive fraction below 1, must give an answer greater than 6/7.
[WorkedStep] His answer, 2/15, is less than 1/2, while 6/7 is greater than 1/2. So 2/15 is smaller than 6/7, the opposite of what we need. We can reject his answer before calculating the division.
[WorkedStep] Now correct it: 6/7 ÷ 3/5 = 6/7 × 5/3 = ((6 ÷ 3) × 5)/(7 × (3 ÷ 3)) = 10/7 = 1 3/7.
[WorkedStep] Check: 10/7 × 3/5 = 30/35 = 6/7.

Practice 2C Question 6
[Question] A lorry has 3/7 tonne of rice. It is packed into bags holding 3/112 tonne each. How many complete bags can be filled? Explain why the answer is a whole number.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] We have 3/7 tonne of rice, and each bag needs 3/112 tonne. Give the total denominator 112: 3/7 = (3 × 16)/(7 × 16) = 48/112 tonne.
[WorkedStep] Think of the total as 48 equal portions, each weighing 1/112 tonne. Each bag needs 3 such portions.
[WorkedStep] 48 ÷ 3 = 16, so there are 16 complete bags. Equivalently, 3/7 ÷ 3/112 = 3/7 × 112/3 = 112/7 = 16.
[WorkedStep] The answer is a whole number because the total contains exactly 16 bag-sized groups, with no rice left. Check: 16 × 3/112 = 48/112 = 3/7 tonne.

[PanelizationMetadata] APPLIES TO: CH02-PAGE057-PANEL02; Visual beat CH02 06E B; location reference; geography and equipment at the assigned stage; assigned beat view and state only
[ProductionNote] Dispenser control reference: the supply tap isolates the brass tank from the measuring cup. The cup’s adjustable stop sets its fill capacity, calibrated in batter mass for this recipe. The long cool-side handle operates the cup outlet; a mechanical interlock closes the tank feed before opening that outlet. At rest the outlet is closed; the supply tap may charge the cup. Lowering the handle isolates the tank and releases only the cup contents. The heater is independent. Use these same three controls in every view. The original stock tray and the separate wrap-filling vessels remain distinct.

[SceneHeading] Scene CH02 07B The first food reaches the Gate
[ProductionLabel] Production instructions are non-printing. Exact reader text is assigned beneath each visual beat.
[ProductionNote] Setting. Location CH02 L04: Outside the Old Blue Gate, two weathered blue timber leaves stand between pale-stone piers, with brass ribs, moon-shaped openings and one round full-moon ornament above. Seen from the lane, the small service doorway is in the left leaf, the bench is right and the planter is left. Same full-moon night. Warm task lamps and cool moonlit edges remain consistent; the current scene controls repaired and unrepaired states.
[ProductionNote] View. Exterior medium from the waiting lane towards the small service door and bench, with blue timber and pale stone visible.
[ProductionNote] Cast and positions. Outside the Gate, Ira stands nearest the small service doorway in the left leaf as seen from the lane; Kabir stands beside her with his ruled notebook. The girl in green waits with her two friends close to them. The green Gate helper controls the doorway. Other waiting children remain behind the group; no parent or human stall worker is present.
[ProductionNote] Props and state progression. The large blue doors remain shut to general admission until the final authorisation. The small service doorway permits supervised messages and food delivery. The separate equipment exit beyond the left pier is not this door. Food-delivery groups do not determine admission groups. Ira’s cup drawing and each later written message are separate sheets. Ira has received Pip’s new update. The first wrap tray arrives with a saffron assistant. There are not yet any drinks from the sixteen-cup delivery. The original cup drawing remains at Food Street.
[ProductionNote] Planning requirements. Do not print the update twice: its exact words appear on the note in Scene CH02 07A; here the source caption describes Ira reading it aloud. No extra speech is invented.

# 2.4 Fractions and Decimals
Fractions such as 1/10, 1/100 and 1/1000 can also be written as decimals: 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001. The dot is the decimal point.
Let’s read 123.456 using the place-value table. The position of each digit tells us its value. Read the headings first: hundreds, tens, ones, tenths, hundredths, thousandths.
| Hundreds | Tens | Ones | Tenths | Hundredths | Thousandths |
| 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| 100 | 20 | 3 | 4/10 | 5/100 | 6/1000 |
[Caption] 123.456 — read the place names from left to right; the decimal point belongs between ones and tenths.
[ProductionNote] Production note V15 — The table represents 123.456. Place a visible decimal-point marker between ones and tenths. Keep the digit and its value vertically aligned. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
In 123.456, read the digits before the point: 1 hundred = 100, 2 tens = 20, and 3 ones = 3.
Now read the digits after the point: 4 tenths = 4/10 = 0.4; 5 hundredths = 5/100 = 0.05; 6 thousandths = 6/1000 = 0.006.
