[PanelizationLabel] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
Example 34
[Question] Amy buys a loaf of bread with a promotional label saying “extra 25%”.
[Question] (a)  What does “extra 25%” mean?
[Question] (b)  Express 25% as a fraction in simplest form.
Let’s work it through
[WorkedStep] (a) “Extra 25%” means the shop adds an amount equal to 25% of the original loaf. In the diagram, the full gold bar represents 1 original loaf. It is divided into 4 equal parts. The teal part is the extra bread.
[WorkedStep] (b) Write 25% as a fraction: 25% = 25/100 = (25 ÷ 25)/(100 ÷ 25) = 1/4. So the extra bread is 1/4 of the original loaf.
[WorkedStep] The original loaf contains 4 quarters. Add the extra quarter: 4/4 + 1/4 = 5/4 = 1 1/4 times the original amount.
[WorkedStep] In percentages, the new total is 100% + 25% = 125% of the original loaf. The 25% labels only the added bread; 125% labels all the bread in the new loaf.
[ProductionLabel] DO NOT PRINT — Figure reference: V32 | The following caption sentence is printable unchanged.
[Caption] Add 1/4 of the original loaf: 1 + 1/4 = 1 1/4.
[ProductionNote] Production note V32 — One usual loaf is a gold bar. Add one teal quarter of that same whole. Total length is1.25times the usual length; do not confuse extra25% with total25%. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
Your turn after Example 34
[Question] A washing-powder packet claims “10% more powder”. Express 10% as a fraction in simplest form.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] 10% = 10/100 = (10 ÷ 10)/(100 ÷ 10) = 1/10. So the extra powder is 1/10 of the usual amount. The new total is 10/10 + 1/10 = 11/10 = 1 1/10 times the usual amount.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE128-PANEL01

## Practice 2J
Practice 2J Question 1
[Question] Express each percentage as a fraction in simplest form.
[Question] (a)  5%
[Question] (b)  32%
[Question] (c)  112%
[Question] (d)  150%
[Question] (e)  2 1/2%
[Question] (f)  12.5%
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  5% = 5/100 = (5 ÷ 5)/(100 ÷ 5) = 1/20.
[WorkedStep] (b)  32% = 32/100 = (32 ÷ 4)/(100 ÷ 4) = 8/25.
[WorkedStep] (c)  112% = 112/100 = (112 ÷ 4)/(100 ÷ 4) = 28/25. This is 28/25 = 1 3/25.
[WorkedStep] (d)  150% = 150/100 = (150 ÷ 50)/(100 ÷ 50) = 3/2. This is 3/2 = 1 1/2.
[WorkedStep] (e)  2 1/2 = (2 × 2 + 1)/2 = 5/2. Now apply the percent sign: divide this number by 100.
[WorkedStep] 2 1/2% = 5/2 × 1/100 = 5/200 = (5 ÷ 5)/(200 ÷ 5) = 1/40.
[WorkedStep] (f) 12.5% = 12.5/100. Multiply top and bottom by 10: 12.5/100 = (12.5 × 10)/(100 × 10) = 125/1000.
[WorkedStep] Simplify: 125/1000 = (125 ÷ 125)/(1000 ÷ 125) = 1/8.
Practice 2J Question 2
[Question] Express each percentage as a decimal.
[Question] (a)  68%
[Question] (b)  95%
[Question] (c)  199%
[Question] (d)  6 1/2%
[Question] (e)  40 1/2%
[Question] (f)  50.7%
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  68% = 68 ÷ 100 = 0.68.
[WorkedStep] (b)  95% = 95 ÷ 100 = 0.95.
[WorkedStep] (c) 199% = 199 ÷ 100 = 1.99. Since 199% is more than 100%, its decimal is more than 1.
[WorkedStep] (d) 6 1/2 = 6.5, so 6 1/2% = 6.5 ÷ 100 = 0.065.
[WorkedStep] (e) 40 1/2 = 40.5, so 40 1/2% = 40.5 ÷ 100 = 0.405.
[WorkedStep] (f)  50.7% = 50.7 ÷ 100 = 0.507.

Practice 2J Question 3
[Question] The box stands for a whole number and 32/(□) = 20%. Is □ (a) more than 100, (b) less than 100, (c) 100, or (d) none of these?
Check your method
[WorkedStep] Start with the percentage: 20% = 20/100 = 1/5. We need 32/(□) to equal 1/5.
[WorkedStep] To turn the numerator 1 into 32, multiply by 32. Multiply the denominator 5 by 32 too: 1/5 = (1 × 32)/(5 × 32) = 32/160.
[WorkedStep] The missing number is 160. Since 160 > 100, choose (a), more than 100. Check: 32/160 = (32 ÷ 32)/(160 ÷ 32) = 1/5 = 20%.
Practice 2J Question 4
[Question] A tea shop offers 40% less sugar in its drinks. Express this percentage.
[Question] (a)  as a fraction in simplest form
[Question] (b)  as a decimal
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  40% = 40/100 = (40 ÷ 20)/(100 ÷ 20) = 2/5.
[WorkedStep] (b)  40% = 40 ÷ 100 = 0.4.
The question asks for the reduction, 40%. If we also want the sugar left, subtract from 100%: 100% − 40% = 60% of the usual amount.
Practice 2J Question 5
[Question] In a 2011 statement, 88.6% of Singapore’s population used public transport. Express this percentage.
[Question] (a)  as a fraction in simplest form
[Question] (b)  as a decimal
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  88.6% = 88.6/100 = (88.6 × 10)/(100 × 10) = 886/1000.
[WorkedStep] Divide top and bottom by 2: 886/1000 = (886 ÷ 2)/(1000 ÷ 2) = 443/500.
[WorkedStep] (b)  88.6% = 88.6 ÷ 100 = 0.886.
Practice 2J Question 6
[Question] 45% of a student’s end-of-year result comes from continual assessment. Express this percentage.
[Question] (a)  as a fraction in simplest form
[Question] (b)  as a decimal
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  45% = 45/100 = (45 ÷ 5)/(100 ÷ 5) = 9/20.
[WorkedStep] (b)  45% = 45 ÷ 100 = 0.45.

[PanelizationLabel] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) 25% = 25/100 = 1/4. Add 1/4 of the usual loaf to 1 usual loaf: 1 + 1/4 = 1 1/4. Diagram II shows that total, so match 25% more to II.
[WorkedStep] (b) 50% = 50/100 = 1/2. Total: 1 + 1/2 = 1 1/2 times the usual loaf. Match I.
[WorkedStep] (c) 150% = 150/100 = 1 1/2. This is the extra amount. Total: 1 + 1 1/2 = 2 1/2 times the usual loaf. Match IV.
[WorkedStep] (d) 200% = 200/100 = 2. This adds 2 usual loaves to the original 1: 1 + 2 = 3. Match III.
[WorkedStep] In every diagram, gold shows the original loaf and teal shows the extra bread. For 150% more, for example, compare the teal length with 1 gold loaf; then include the gold loaf to get the total.
[ProductionLabel] DO NOT PRINT — Figure reference: V34 | The following caption sentence is printable unchanged.
[Caption] Gold represents the usual amount; teal is extra.
[ProductionNote] Production note V34 — Preserve diagramsI,II,III,IV at total lengths1.5,1.25,3,2.5times one whole. Add matched percentage-increase labels. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.

# 2.9 Converting a Fraction or Decimal to a Percentage
We have travelled from percentages to fractions and decimals. Now let’s reverse the journey. If 10 sweets out of 150 are green, the fraction is 10/150. How could we describe that share “out of 100”? We will try it with a collection, then turn the idea into a calculation.
## Knowledge Building Task
Work in a group of five if possible. Use a packet of sweets with five or more colours. Count all the sweets first, then count each colour. Do not eat any until the counts are recorded, or the whole may quietly get smaller!
Open a spreadsheet. Each box is called a cell. Its name gives its column and row: F1 means column F, row 1. Put the total number of sweets in F1. Put the colour names across row 2, starting at B2, and each colour’s count directly below it in row 3.
The sample uses five colours. If your packet has more, continue the colour columns to the right. Keep the total in F1; every sweet must appear in exactly one colour count.

[PanelizationLabel] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
1. In the sample, F1 holds 150 sweets and B3 holds 10 green sweets. Click B4 and type =B$3/$F$1, then press Enter. The / means divide, so the formula calculates 10 ÷ 150.
The dollar signs help when we copy this formula: B$3 keeps row 3 for the count; $F$1 keeps cell F1 for the total. Here $ is a spreadsheet instruction, not a money sign.
2. Copy the formula from B4 into B5 and B6. All three cells now calculate 10 ÷ 150. We will show that same value in three different ways.
3. Select B4 and choose Fraction format, allowing up to 3 digits in the denominator. Select B5 and choose Number format with 2 decimal places. Select B6 and choose Percentage format with 2 decimal places. The menu names may vary between spreadsheets.
4. Select the three cells B4, B5 and B6 together. Copy them across to the other colour columns, C through F. In C4, for example, the formula becomes =C$3/$F$1: the brown count divided by the same total.
Let’s check the green sweets: 10/150 = (10 ÷ 10)/(150 ÷ 10) = 1/15 = 0.06666… . B4 shows 1/15, B5 shows 0.07 and B6 shows 6.67%.
Why not 7%? The decimal display 0.07 is rounded. The formula still uses 10 ÷ 150, giving 6.666…%, which rounds to 6.67%.
Keep the formula in each cell. Typing 0.07 instead would give 0.07 × 100% = 7%. Also, do not add ×100 to the formula: Percentage format already makes that display change.
Enter the remaining colour counts in row 3. Do they add up to the total in F1? Now look at the percentages in row 6. What should all the colours add up to? Explain before checking below.

[PanelizationLabel] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
Check your method
All the colours together make all the sweets: 150/150 = 1 whole = 100%. So the percentages add to 100% before rounding.
Our unfinished sample shows only 10 green sweets, so it does not yet total 100%. Once every count is entered, rounding may make the displayed percentages total 99.99% or 100.01%. Check the counts and the unrounded values before declaring a sweet missing!
Now look at the next rectangle. It represents 1 whole, and exactly half is shaded. The shaded amount can be written as 1/2, as 0.5, or as 50%. The picture stays the same; only its name changes.
[ProductionLabel] DO NOT PRINT — Figure reference: V36 | The following caption sentence is printable unchanged.
[Caption] The shaded half is 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%.
[ProductionNote] Production note V36 — One rectangle with exactly one half shaded. Beneath show1/2=0.5=50%; a second line shows0.5×100%=50%. Distinguish percent sign from plain multiplication by100; do not show different shaded quantities. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
Why multiply a fraction by 100%? One whole is 100%, so half a whole is 1/2 × 100% = 50%. Three quarters of a whole is 3/4 × 100% = 75%.
Keep the % sign with 50: 1/2 = 50%, because 50% means 50/100. The number 50 on its own would mean 50 wholes!

Example 35
[Question] Convert each fraction to a percentage.
[Question] (a)  1/2
[Question] (b)  1 3/4
Let’s work it through
[WorkedStep] (a)  One whole is 100%. Split it into 2 equal halves: 100% ÷ 2 = 50%. So 1/2 = 50%, or 1/2 × 100% = 50%.
[WorkedStep] (b) First change 1 3/4 to an improper fraction:
[WorkedStep] 1 3/4 = (1 × 4 + 3)/4 = 7/4.
[WorkedStep] Now multiply by 100%: 7/4 × 100% = 7 × (100 ÷ 4)% = 7 × 25% = 175%.
[WorkedStep] Check: 1 < 1 3/4 < 2, and 100% < 175% < 200%.
Your turn after Example 35
[Question] Convert each fraction to a percentage.
[Question] (a)  1/5
[Question] (b)  2 1/8
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  1/5 × 100% = (100 ÷ 5)% = 20%.
[WorkedStep] (b) Change the mixed number first: 2 1/8 = (2 × 8 + 1)/8 = 17/8.
[WorkedStep] Then 17/8 × 100% = 17 × (100 ÷ 8)% = 17 × 12.5% = 212.5%, or 212 1/2%.
[WorkedStep] A percentage can have a decimal or fraction part, as 212.5% does here.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE137-PANEL01

Example 36
[Question] Convert each decimal to a percentage.
[Question] (a)  0.8
[Question] (b)  1.15
Let’s work it through
[WorkedStep] (a) 0.8 means 8 tenths: 0.8 = 8/10. Write it in hundredths: 8/10 = (8 × 10)/(10 × 10) = 80/100. So 0.8 = 80%.
[WorkedStep] The shorter calculation is 0.8 × 100% = 80%.
[WorkedStep] (b) 1.15 means 1 whole and 15 hundredths. One whole is 100 hundredths, so 1.15 = (100 + 15)/100 = 115/100 = 115%.
[WorkedStep] The shorter calculation is 1.15 × 100% = 115%. The percentage is above 100% because 1.15 is above 1.
Your turn after Example 36
[Question] Convert each decimal to a percentage.
[Question] (a)  0.06
[Question] (b)  3.2
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  0.06 × 100% = 6%. Six hundredths is six out of a hundred.
[WorkedStep] (b)  3.2 × 100% = 320%. The value is more than three wholes, so the percentage is more than 300%.

## Practice 2K
Practice 2K Question 1
[Question] Convert each fraction to a percentage.
[Question] (a)  4/5
[Question] (b)  2/3
[Question] (c)  1/8
[Question] (d)  1 5/6
[Question] (e)  10/3
[Question] (f)  25/4
[Question] (g)  13/100
[Question] (h)  1 1/100
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) 4/5 × 100% = 400/5% = 80%.
[WorkedStep] (b) 2/3 × 100% = 200/3%. Now 200 ÷ 3 = 66 remainder 2, giving exactly 66 2/3%.
[WorkedStep] Keep the fraction: 66.666…% never stops, and a rounded decimal would no longer be exact.
[WorkedStep] (c) 1/8 × 100% = 100/8% = 12.5%, or 12 1/2%.
[WorkedStep] (d) 1 5/6 = (1 × 6 + 5)/6 = 11/6. Then 11/6 × 100% = 1100/6% = 183 2/6% = 183 1/3%.
[WorkedStep] (e) 10/3 × 100% = 1000/3% = 333 1/3%.
[WorkedStep] (f) 25/4 × 100% = 2500/4% = 625%.
[WorkedStep] (g) 13/100 × 100% = 13%.
[WorkedStep] (h) 1 1/100 = 101/100, so 101/100 × 100% = 101%.

Practice 2K Question 2
[Question] Convert each decimal to a percentage.
[Question] (a)  0.14
[Question] (b)  0.04
[Question] (c)  1.25
[Question] (d)  0.75
[Question] (e)  0.01
[Question] (f)  3.1
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  0.14 × 100% = 14%.

Practice 2K Question 4
[Question] In a Mathematics exam, 3/4 of the marks come from the Short-Answer Question Section and 1/4 from the Long-Answer Question Section. What percentage comes from each?
[Question] (a)  Short-Answer Question Section
[Question] (b)  Long-Answer Question Section
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) Short-Answer Question Section: 3/4 × 100% = 3 × (100 ÷ 4)% = 3 × 25% = 75%.
[WorkedStep] (b) Long-Answer Question Section: 1/4 × 100% = (100 ÷ 4)% = 25%. Check: 75% + 25% = 100%, covering all the marks.
Practice 2K Question 5
[Question] A box contains red and blue balls. Of all the balls, 9/20 are red and 11/20 are blue. What percentage is each colour?
[Question] (a)  Red
[Question] (b)  Blue
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) Red balls: 9/20 × 100% = 9 × (100 ÷ 20)% = 9 × 5% = 45%.
[WorkedStep] (b) Blue balls: 11/20 × 100% = 11 × (100 ÷ 20)% = 11 × 5% = 55%. Check: 45% + 55% = 100%.

[Question] (b)  Phone bill

[WorkedStep] (a)  1/5 × 100% = 20%.
[WorkedStep] (b) Phone bill: 1/4 × 100% = 25%.

Practice 2K Question 7
[Question] Saiful must arrange 13%, 1/8, 26%, 1/4, 0.32, 5/8 and 60% in ascending order.
[Question] (a)  How would you advise him to approach the problem?
[Question] (b)  Arrange the numbers in ascending order.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) Write every value as a percentage so that we compare the same kind of number. Leave 13%, 26% and 60% unchanged. Convert the fractions and the decimal as shown below. Use the original forms when writing the final order.
[WorkedStep] (b) 1/8 × 100% = (100 ÷ 8)% = 12.5%.
[WorkedStep] 1/4 × 100% = (100 ÷ 4)% = 25%.
[WorkedStep] 0.32 × 100% = 32%.
[WorkedStep] 5/8 × 100% = 5 × (100 ÷ 8)% = 5 × 12.5% = 62.5%.
[WorkedStep] Compare: 12.5% < 13% < 25% < 26% < 32% < 60% < 62.5%.
[WorkedStep] Ascending order: 1/8, 13%, 1/4, 26%, 0.32, 60%, 5/8.

# 2.10 Expressing a Quantity as a Percentage of Another
We have changed given fractions into percentages. Next we will build the fraction ourselves. Suppose 2 counters are selected from a group of 10 counters. The diagram shows all 10 counters; the 2 selected counters are coloured differently.
All 10 counters make the total, so put 10 underneath. The 2 selected counters go on top: 2 out of 10 is 2/10.
[ProductionLabel] DO NOT PRINT — Figure reference: V39 | The following caption sentence is printable unchanged.
[Caption] 2 selected counters out of 10: 2/10 = 20%.
[ProductionNote] Production note V39 — Show two selected counters among ten, plus a labelled bar where10 corresponds to100% and2 to20%. Label top quantity2 and reference10; retain equal counter sizes. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
2 as a percentage of 10 = 2/10 × 100% = 2 × 10% = 20%.
Always finish the question “percentage of what?” In “2 as a percentage of 10”, the answer is “of 10”, so 10 goes underneath.
For example, 50% of 40 minutes means half of 40 minutes: 40 ÷ 2 = 20 minutes. But 50% of 80 marks means half of 80 marks: 80 ÷ 2 = 40 marks. The same 50% can describe different amounts because the starting amounts differ.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE143-PANEL01

[PanelizationLabel] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
The two quantities in our fraction must use the same unit. For “9 cents as a percentage of $1.50”, first change $1.50 to 150 cents. Then compare 9 cents with 150 cents. Let’s do that carefully.
Example 37
[Question] Express each as a percentage.
[Question] (a)  5 as a percentage of 10
[Question] (b)  9 cents as a percentage of $1.50
Let’s work it through
[WorkedStep] (a)  The whole we compare with is 10. We have 5 of those 10, so the fraction is 5/10 = 1/2. Half of 100% is 50%, so 5 is 50% of 10.
[WorkedStep] (b)  First match the units. We cannot compare 9 cents with the number 1.50 as though it also meant cents. One dollar is 100 cents, so $1.50 = 100 cents + 50 cents = 150 cents.
[WorkedStep] The fraction is 9/150. Multiply by 100%: 9/150 × 100% = 900/150% = 6%, since 150 × 6 = 900. Check: 1% of 150 cents is 1.5 cents, and 6 × 1.5 cents = 9 cents.
Your turn after Example 37
[Question] Express each as a percentage.
[Question] (a)  8 as a percentage of 20
[Question] (b)  45 cm as a percentage of 1.2 m
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  8/20 × 100% = 8 × (100 ÷ 20)% = 8 × 5% = 40%.
[WorkedStep] (b) We are comparing 45 cm with 1.2 m. First change 1.2 m to centimetres: 1.2 × 100 cm = 120 cm.
[WorkedStep] Now both lengths use centimetres. The fraction is 45/120, so the percentage is 45/120 × 100% = 4500/120% = 37.5%.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE144-PANEL01

[WorkedStep] For a group of equal items, we can also find one item’s percentage first. Let’s compare that route with the fraction method.
Example 38
[Question] In a class of 25 students, 10 wear spectacles. Find each percentage using two methods, and compare the methods.
[Question] (a)  Students who wear spectacles
[Question] (b)  Students who do not wear spectacles
Let’s work it through
[WorkedStep] (a)  Method 1 uses a fraction of the class. Ten of the 25 students wear spectacles, so 10/25 × 100% = 10 × (100 ÷ 25)% = 10 × 4% = 40%.
[WorkedStep] Method 2 finds one student's share first. All 25 students represent 100%. Divide equally: 100% ÷ 25 = 4% per student. Then 10 students represent 10 × 4% = 40%.
[WorkedStep] (b) Method 1: first count the students without spectacles. There are 25 − 10 = 15. Their percentage is 15/25 × 100% = 15 × (100 ÷ 25)% = 15 × 4% = 60%.
[WorkedStep] Method 2: the whole class is 100%, and 40% wear spectacles. So the percentage without spectacles is 100% − 40% = 60%. This is shorter once we know 40%.
[WorkedStep] Both methods give 60%. Check: 40% + 60% = 100%, so the two groups include all 25 students.
Your turn after Example 38
[Question] In a class of 40 students, 28 belong to the swimming team. Find each percentage using two methods.
[Question] (a)  Students in the swimming team
[Question] (b)  Students not in the swimming team
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) Method 1: compare the 28 team members with all 40 students: 28/40 × 100% = 2800/40% = 70%.
[WorkedStep] Method 2: 1 student represents 100% ÷ 40 = 2.5%. So 28 students represent 28 × 2.5% = 70%.
[WorkedStep] (b) Method 1: 40 − 28 = 12 students are not in the team. Their percentage is 12/40 × 100% = 1200/40% = 30%.
[WorkedStep] Method 2: subtract the team’s percentage from 100%: 100% − 70% = 30%. Check: 70% + 30% = 100%.

Example 39
[Question] A basket contains 20 fruits. Eight are apples and the rest are oranges.
[Question] (a)  What percentage are apples?
[Question] (b)  What percentage are oranges?
Let’s work it through
[WorkedStep] (a) The basket contains 20 fruits in all, so use 20 underneath. The 8 apples represent 8/20 × 100% = 8 × (100 ÷ 20)% = 8 × 5% = 40%.
[WorkedStep] (b) Count the oranges: 20 − 8 = 12. Their percentage is 12/20 × 100% = 12 × 5% = 60%.
[WorkedStep] Or subtract the apples’ share from the whole basket: 100% − 40% = 60%. This works because every fruit is either an apple or an orange.
Your turn after Example 39
[Question] A shopping mall has 60 shops. Of these, 45 are eateries and the rest are non-eateries.
[Question] (a)  What percentage are eateries?
[Question] (b)  What percentage are non-eateries?
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) Eateries: 45/60 × 100% = (45 ÷ 15)/(60 ÷ 15) × 100% = 3/4 × 100% = 75%.
[WorkedStep] (b) There are 60 − 45 = 15 non-eateries. Their percentage is 15/60 × 100% = 1/4 × 100% = 25%. Check: 100% − 75% = 25%.

[PanelizationLabel] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
## Comparing Two Quantities by Percentage
Nurul and Linda each save $300 a month. Does that mean each saves the same percentage of her income? We need their incomes to answer that.
Nurul earns $3000 a month; Linda earns $600. Compare Nurul’s $300 with her $3000, and Linda’s $300 with her $600.
In the diagram, each full bar represents 100% of that person’s income. The bars have the same drawn length, but they represent different amounts of money: $3000 for Nurul and $600 for Linda. The shaded part of each bar represents the $300 saved.
[ProductionLabel] DO NOT PRINT — Figure reference: V41 | The following caption sentence is printable unchanged.
[Caption] Both save $300. Compare it with each person’s income.
[ProductionNote] Production note V41 — Two equal-length percentage bars represent separate wholes, labelled Nurul income$3000 and Linda income$600. Shade10% and50% respectively, both labelled saving$300. Explicitly state same bar length represents100% of each separate income, not equal dollars. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
Nurul: 300/3000 × 100% = 1/10 × 100% = 10%.
Linda: 300/600 × 100% = 1/2 × 100% = 50%.
Linda saves the larger percentage: 50% > 10%. The same $300 is half of Linda’s $600, but only one tenth of Nurul’s $3000. This compares their savings with their incomes; it does not tell us whose expenses make saving easier.

Example 40
[Question] Class A has 25 students and 10 receive gold awards in a fitness test. Class B has 40 students and 12 receive gold awards. Which class does better by the percentage receiving gold?
Let’s work it through
[WorkedStep] Class A has 10 gold-award students out of 25 students: 10/25 × 100% = 1000/25% = 40%.
[WorkedStep] Class B has 12 gold-award students out of 40 students: 12/40 × 100% = 1200/40% = 30%.
[WorkedStep] Since 40% > 30%, Class A does better by the percentage receiving gold. Class B has more gold awards, 12 rather than 10, but it also has more students, 40 rather than 25. That is why we compare each award count with its own class total.
Your turn after Example 40
[Question] A 100 g bag of chips contains 20 g of fibre. A 150 g bag of cereal contains 75 g of fibre. Which food contains a greater percentage of fibre?
Check your method
[WorkedStep] Chips: compare 20 g of fibre with the 100 g bag: 20/100 × 100% = 20%.
[WorkedStep] Cereal: compare 75 g of fibre with the 150 g bag: 75/150 × 100% = 1/2 × 100% = 50%.
[WorkedStep] Since 50% > 20%, cereal contains the greater percentage of fibre. Each denominator is the mass of that food’s own bag.

## Practice 2L
Practice 2L Question 1
[Question] Express each as a percentage.
[Question] (a)  3 as a percentage of 10
[Question] (b)  30 as a percentage of 60
[Question] (c)  10 1/2 as a percentage of 21
[Question] (d)  1 1/4 as a percentage of 24
[Question] (e)  1.8 as a percentage of 18
[Question] (f)  59.5 as a percentage of 238
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  We compare 3 with 10, so put 10 underneath: 3/10 × 100% = 3 × (100 ÷ 10)% = 30%.
[WorkedStep] (b)  30/60 = (30 ÷ 30)/(60 ÷ 30) = 1/2. Then 1/2 × 100% = 50%.
[WorkedStep] (c) First change the mixed number: 10 1/2 = (10 × 2 + 1)/2 = 21/2.
[WorkedStep] We are comparing this amount with 21, so divide by 21: 21/2 ÷ 21 = 21/2 × 1/21 = 21/42 = 1/2.
[WorkedStep] Now convert to a percentage: 1/2 × 100% = 50%. Check: 21 ÷ 2 = 10 1/2, so the given amount is half of 21.
[WorkedStep] (d) Change 1 1/4 to (1 × 4 + 1)/4 = 5/4. We need this amount as a share of 24, so divide by 24:
[WorkedStep] 5/4 ÷ 24 = 5/4 × 1/24 = 5/96.
[WorkedStep] Now change that share to a percentage: 5/96 × 100% = 500/96% = 125/24%, dividing 500 and 96 by 4.
[WorkedStep] Since 125 ÷ 24 = 5 remainder 5, the answer is 5 5/24%.
[WorkedStep] (e)  The amount is decimal, but the meaning is unchanged: 1.8/18 = (1.8 × 10)/(18 × 10) = 18/180 = 1/10. Then 1/10 × 100% = 10%.
[WorkedStep] (f) Notice that 59.5 × 4 = 238. So 59.5 is one quarter of 238: 59.5/238 = 1/4. Then 1/4 × 100% = 25%.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE149-PANEL01

Practice 2L Question 2
[Question] Express each as a percentage. Convert to matching units first where needed.
[Question] (a)  26 cm of 100 cm
[Question] (b)  10 g of 250 g
[Question] (c)  3 kg of 15 kg
[Question] (d)  45 cents of 90 cents
[Question] (e)  35 cents of $1
[Question] (f)  510 mL of 1 L
[Question] (g)  12 cents of $1.20
[Question] (h)  340 g of 1 kg
[Question] (i)  200 g of 1200 g
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  26/100 × 100% = 26%.
[WorkedStep] (b)  10/250 × 100% = 1000/250% = 4%.
[WorkedStep] (c)  3/15 × 100% = 1/5 × 100% = 20%, dividing 3 and 15 by 3 first.
[WorkedStep] (d)  45/90 × 100% = 1/2 × 100% = 50%, dividing 45 and 90 by 45 first.
[WorkedStep] (e)  $1 = 100 cents. Then 35/100 × 100% = 35%.
[WorkedStep] (f)  1 L = 1000 mL. Then 510/1000 × 100% = 51%.
[WorkedStep] (g)  $1.20 = 120 cents. Then 12/120 × 100% = 10%.
[WorkedStep] (h)  1 kg = 1000 g. Then 340/1000 × 100% = 34%.
[WorkedStep] (i)  200/1200 = (200 ÷ 200)/(1200 ÷ 200) = 1/6. Then 1/6 × 100% = 100/6% = 16 4/6% = 16 2/3%, since 100 = 16 × 6 + 4.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE150-PANEL01

Practice 2L Question 3
[Question] A class has 40 students, including 15 boys. Find the percentage who are
[Question] (a)  boys
[Question] (b)  girls
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) Boys: 15/40 × 100% = 1500/40% = 37.5%.
[WorkedStep] (b) Girls: 40 − 15 = 25. Their percentage is 25/40 × 100% = 2500/40% = 62.5%. Check: 37.5% + 62.5% = 100%.
Practice 2L Question 4
[Question] A bottle holds 1 L when full and contains 680 mL of water. Find the percentage of its capacity that is
[Question] (a)  filled with water
[Question] (b)  empty
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  1 L = 1000 mL. Then 680/1000 × 100% = 68%.
[WorkedStep] (b) Empty capacity = 1000 − 680 = 320 mL. Then 320/1000 × 100% = 32%.
Practice 2L Question 5
[Question] A crate contains 60 apples, of which 12 are rotten. Find the percentage that are
[Question] (a)  rotten
[Question] (b)  not rotten
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  12/60 × 100% = 20%.
[WorkedStep] (b) 60 − 12 = 48 apples are not rotten. Then 48/60 × 100% = 80%.

Practice 2L Question 6
[Question] Benny spends 8 hours in the office, including a 1-hour lunch break and a 1/2-hour tea break. He works for the remaining time. Find the percentage of the 8 hours spent on
[Question] (a)  lunch
[Question] (b)  tea break
[Question] (c)  work
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) Lunch takes 1 of the 8 hours: 1/8 × 100% = (100 ÷ 8)% = 12.5%.
[WorkedStep] (b) The tea break is 1/2 hour = 0.5 hour. Its share is 0.5/8 × 100% = 50/8% = 6.25%.
[WorkedStep] (c) Work time = 8 − 1 − 0.5 = 6.5 hours. Its share is 6.5/8 × 100% = 650/8% = 81.25%.
[WorkedStep] Check: 12.5% + 6.25% + 81.25% = 100%. We divide by the full 8 hours in every part, including the breaks in that total.
Practice 2L Question 7
[Question] The pet table lists these numbers of families in a town: goldfish 100, hamster 150, rabbit 250, cat 500.
[Question] (a)  Find the percentage keeping cats.
[Question] (b)  Find the percentage keeping goldfish.
[Question] (c)  Find the difference between the percentages keeping hamsters and rabbits.
| Pet | Number of families |
| Goldfish | 100 |
| Hamster | 150 |
| Rabbit | 250 |
| Cat | 500 |
[ProductionNote] Production note V42 — Preserve the four categories and counts; do not add a total to the question table. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) For this exercise, assume each family appears in just one of the four pet groups. Add the counts to find the total: 100 + 150 + 250 + 500 = 1000 families.
[WorkedStep] Cats: 500/1000 × 100% = 50%.
[WorkedStep] (b)  Goldfish: 100/1000 × 100% = 10%.
[WorkedStep] (c)  Hamsters: 150/1000 × 100% = 15%. Rabbits: 250/1000 × 100% = 25%.
[WorkedStep] Difference: 25% − 15% = 10 percentage points. We use “percentage points” for the gap between two percentages.
[WorkedStep] In a real survey, one family might keep both a cat and a rabbit. Adding the pet-group counts would then count that family twice. We would need the number of different families before finding percentages of all families.

Practice 2L Question 8
[Question] Decide whether each statement is true or false. For a true statement, give an example. For a false statement, explain and give the correct statement.
[Question] (a)  Class A has twice as many students as Class B. Therefore Class B has 1/2 as many students as Class A.
[Question] (b)  Class A has 60% as many students as Class B. Therefore Class B has 1/60% as many students as Class A.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  True. If Class A has twice as many students as Class B, Class B has half as many as A. For example, take B = 20 and A = 40. Then 40 = 2 × 20, while 20 = 1/2 × 40. Reversing the comparison changes “twice” to “half”.
[WorkedStep] (b) Let’s try Class B with 50 students. Class A has 60% of 50: 60/100 × 50 = 3/5 × 50 = 3 × 10 = 30 students. These are example class sizes.
[WorkedStep] Now compare B’s 50 students with A’s 30 students. We want B as a percentage of A, so put 30 underneath:
[WorkedStep] 50/30 × 100% = 5/3 × 100% = 500/3% = 166 2/3%.
[WorkedStep] The claim is false. Class B has 166 2/3% as many students as Class A. That is more than 100%, which fits: B is the larger class.
[WorkedStep] The same answer works for other class sizes too: 60% = 3/5, so A has 3 students for every 5 in B. Reversing the comparison gives 5/3, as in 50/30 = 5/3 above.
[WorkedStep] Keep an eye on “of”: A as a percentage of B uses 30/50; B as a percentage of A uses 50/30. Same classes, different comparison.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE152-PANEL01

[PanelizationMetadata] SOURCE: Location CH02 L03 Food Street — Packing Bench and Balanced Loading Table
[PanelizationMetadata] APPLIES TO: CH02-PAGE153-PANEL01; Visual beat CH02 12I A; location reference; geography and equipment at the assigned stage; assigned beat view and state only
[ProductionNote] The upper carrier is a four-by-four arrangement of sixteen cup places. The lower shelf’s MAXIMUM LOAD 4.5 kg label belongs only to that shelf. The table has a fixed pedestal, a rotating head and a centrally pivoted two-tray cradle. Its one accessible brake housing has a rotation latch and a squeeze lever linked to the cradle’s tilt damper. The latch holds rotation from Visual beat CH02 01B C to CH02 13D A; it does not clamp the cradle. Squeezing the lever damps sudden tilt while held; it does not rigidly lock the cradle angle. Mechanical travel stops limit the dip; no tray falls. The original cup drawing is clipped above the bench from Scene CH02 02D until Scene CH02 14A. After dispatch its former clip is empty. Use exact dedicated count diagrams for the pack states; do not demand tiny exact counts in every scenic wide.

# Chapter 2 Key Ideas
We have written amounts as fractions, decimals and percentages. For example, 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%: three ways to name the same half. Before the revision, let’s bring the main methods together with numbers you can follow.
## Fractions
For 2 1/4 + 1 1/2, first give the fraction parts the same denominator: 1/2 = (1 × 2)/(2 × 2) = 2/4.
Add the whole-number parts, 2 + 1 = 3, and the fraction parts, 1/4 + 2/4 = 3/4. So 2 1/4 + 1 1/2 = 3 3/4.
For 4 1/3 − 2 1/6, change 1/3 to sixths: 1/3 = (1 × 2)/(3 × 2) = 2/6. Now subtract the whole-number parts, 4 − 2 = 2, and the fraction parts, 2/6 − 1/6 = 1/6.
Thus 4 1/3 − 2 1/6 = 4 2/6 − 2 1/6 = 2 1/6.
For multiplication, multiply the top numbers and multiply the bottom numbers. Here is an example:
5/6 × 7/8 = (5 × 7)/(6 × 8) = 35/48.
For division, keep the first fraction unchanged and multiply by the reciprocal of the second fraction. In 4/9 ÷ 2/3, keep 4/9 and turn 2/3 into 3/2:
4/9 ÷ 2/3 = 4/9 × 3/2 = (2 × 1)/(3 × 1) = 2/3. Here we divided 4 and 2 by 2, and 3 and 9 by 3.

## Decimals and Percentages
To change a fraction to a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator. For 3/8, divide 3 by 8:
3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.
For a mixed number, you can first change it to an improper fraction: 2 1/10 = (2 × 10 + 1)/10 = 21/10 = 21 ÷ 10 = 2.1.
To change a decimal to a fraction, use its place value. The number 0.35 means 35 hundredths, so write 35 over 100, then simplify:
0.35 = 35/100 = (35 ÷ 5)/(100 ÷ 5) = 7/20
5/8 = 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625
2.3 = 2 3/10
In a mixed calculation, do brackets first, then powers and roots, then multiplication and division from left to right, and finally addition and subtraction from left to right. For example, 3.5 + 2 × 1.4 = 3.5 + 2.8 = 6.3.
For addition and subtraction, line up matching place values: 2.3 + 0.45 becomes 2.30 + 0.45 = 2.75. Check by subtracting: 2.75 − 0.45 = 2.30.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE155-PANEL01

The table below collects the conversion methods. Follow the example 1/4 = 0.25 = 25% as you read the different routes.
[ProductionLabel] DO NOT PRINT — Figure reference: V44 | The following caption sentence is printable unchanged.
[Caption] Each route changes the form, not the amount.
[ProductionNote] Production note V44 — Exact mapping table: fraction to decimal numerator÷denominator; decimal to fraction place-value denominator then simplify; percentage to fraction divide by100 then simplify; percentage to decimal divide percentage number by100; fraction/decimal to percentage multiply by100%. Include1/4=0.25=25%. Avoid ambiguous arrows saying divideby100% without explaining numerical convention. Use the current ChandRush colour and design style wherever it supports understanding. If that style would reduce clarity, retain the teaching colours, contrast and mathematical design required here. Mathematical accuracy and comprehension take priority.
To express one quantity as a percentage of another, put the first quantity on top and the quantity after “of” underneath. Match the units, then multiply by 100%.
For example, 45 cm as a percentage of 1.2 m needs 1.2 m = 120 cm first. Then 45/120 × 100% = 37.5%.
A greater percentage need not mean more money or more objects when the totals differ. For example, 50% of 10 is 5, but 20% of 100 is 20. Always read the amount after “of”.

# Chapter 2 Revision
Try each question before reading its worked answer. If you get stuck, ask what you need to do: compare numbers, add amounts, change their form or find a percentage. Then choose the method that fits.
Revision Question 1
[Question] Circle the greater fraction in each pair.
[Question] (a)  5/4, 7/6
[Question] (b)  6/5, 13/10
[Question] (c)  8/7, 27/20
[Question] (d)  12/13, 20/17
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  Use denominator 12 for both fractions: 5/4 = (5 × 3)/(4 × 3) = 15/12, 7/6 = (7 × 2)/(6 × 2) = 14/12.
[WorkedStep] Since 15/12 > 14/12, circle 5/4, the greater fraction.
[WorkedStep] (b)  Use denominator 10 for both fractions: 6/5 = (6 × 2)/(5 × 2) = 12/10.
[WorkedStep] Since 12/10 < 13/10, circle 13/10, the greater fraction.
[WorkedStep] (c) Use denominator 140: 8/7 = (8 × 20)/(7 × 20) = 160/140, 27/20 = (27 × 7)/(20 × 7) = 189/140.
[WorkedStep] Since 160/140 < 189/140, circle 27/20, the greater fraction.
[WorkedStep] (d) Compare each fraction with 1. Since 12 < 13, 12/13 < 1. Since 20 > 17, 20/17 > 1.
[WorkedStep] So 12/13 < 1 < 20/17. Circle 20/17. No common denominator is needed here.

Revision Question 2
[Question] Arrange 5/3, 10/7 and 2 in ascending order.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] 5/3 = 1 2/3 and 10/7 = 1 3/7; both are less than 2.
[WorkedStep] Compare 2/3 = (2 × 7)/(3 × 7) = 14/21 and 3/7 = (3 × 3)/(7 × 3) = 9/21. Since 9/21 < 14/21, ascending order is 10/7, 5/3, 2.
Revision Question 3
[Question] Arrange 12/5, 17/10 and 2 1/10 in descending order.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] Write 12/5 = 2 2/5. Change its fraction part to tenths: 2/5 = (2 × 2)/(5 × 2) = 4/10, so 12/5 = 2 4/10. Also, 17/10 = 1 7/10.
[WorkedStep] Compare 2 4/10 > 2 1/10 > 1 7/10. Descending order: 12/5, 2 1/10, 17/10.
Revision Question 4
[Question] Evaluate and give answers in simplest form.
[Question] (a)  2 1/3 + 1 2/3
[Question] (b)  1 4/5 + 3 3/5
[Question] (c)  2 1/6 + 1 5/12
[Question] (d)  3 1/7 + 1 5/14
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) 2 1/3 + 1 2/3 = 3 + (1 + 2)/3 = 3 + 1 = 4.
[WorkedStep] (b) 1 4/5 + 3 3/5 = 4 + 7/5 = 4 + 1 2/5 = 5 2/5.
[WorkedStep] (c) 1/6 = (1 × 2)/(6 × 2) = 2/12. So 2 1/6 + 1 5/12 = 3 + (2 + 5)/12 = 3 7/12.
[WorkedStep] (d) 1/7 = (1 × 2)/(7 × 2) = 2/14. So 3 1/7 + 1 5/14 = 4 + 7/14. Simplify 7/14 = (7 ÷ 7)/(14 ÷ 7) = 1/2, giving 4 1/2.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE157-PANEL01

Revision Question 5
[Question] Evaluate and give answers in simplest form.
[Question] (a)  3 1/3 + 2 2/5
[Question] (b)  4 5/6 + 5 3/4
[Question] (c)  1 1/24 + 5 5/8
[Question] (d)  3 2/9 + 1 5/12
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  Use denominator 15: 1/3 = (1 × 5)/(3 × 5) = 5/15 and 2/5 = (2 × 3)/(5 × 3) = 6/15.
[WorkedStep] 3 1/3 + 2 2/5 = 5 + 5/15 + 6/15 = 5 + 11/15.
[WorkedStep] Answer: 5 11/15.
[WorkedStep] (b)  Use denominator 12: 5/6 = (5 × 2)/(6 × 2) = 10/12 and 3/4 = (3 × 3)/(4 × 3) = 9/12.
[WorkedStep] 4 5/6 + 5 3/4 = 9 + 10/12 + 9/12 = 9 + 19/12.
[WorkedStep] 19/12 = 1 7/12, so 9 + 1 7/12 = 10 7/12.
[WorkedStep] (c)  Use denominator 24: 1/24 and 5/8 = (5 × 3)/(8 × 3) = 15/24.
[WorkedStep] 1 1/24 + 5 5/8 = 6 + 1/24 + 15/24 = 6 + 16/24.
[WorkedStep] Simplify: 16/24 = (16 ÷ 8)/(24 ÷ 8) = 2/3.
[WorkedStep] Answer: 6 2/3.
[WorkedStep] (d)  Use denominator 36: 2/9 = (2 × 4)/(9 × 4) = 8/36 and 5/12 = (5 × 3)/(12 × 3) = 15/36.
[WorkedStep] 3 2/9 + 1 5/12 = 4 + 8/36 + 15/36 = 4 + 23/36.
[WorkedStep] Answer: 4 23/36.

Revision Question 6
[Question] Evaluate and give answers in simplest form.
[Question] (a)  4/5 × 2/5
[Question] (b)  2/5 × 1/7
[Question] (c)  5/9 × 31/35
[Question] (d)  1/8 × 4/15
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  4/5 × 2/5 = (4 × 2)/(5 × 5) = 8/25.
[WorkedStep] (b)  2/5 × 1/7 = (2 × 1)/(5 × 7) = 2/35.
[WorkedStep] (c) Divide 5 and 35 by 5 before multiplying: 5/9 × 31/35 = (1 × 31)/(9 × 7) = 31/63.
[WorkedStep] (d) Divide 4 and 8 by 4: 1/8 × 4/15 = (1 × 1)/(2 × 15) = 1/30.
Revision Question 7
[Question] Evaluate and give answers in simplest form.
[Question] (a)  4/5 ÷ 2/3
[Question] (b)  2/5 ÷ 1/3
[Question] (c)  7/9 ÷ 2/3
[Question] (d)  9/10 ÷ 4/5
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) 4/5 ÷ 2/3 = 4/5 × 3/2. Divide 4 and 2 by 2: (2 × 3)/(5 × 1) = 6/5 = 1 1/5.

[WorkedStep] (d) 9/10 ÷ 4/5 = 9/10 × 5/4. Divide 5 and 10 by 5: (9 × 1)/(2 × 4) = 9/8 = 1 1/8.

Revision Question 8
[Question] Express the fractions as decimals.
[Question] (a)  14/16
[Question] (b)  45/30
[Question] (c)  117/26
[Question] (d)  2 4/20
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  14/16 = (14 ÷ 2)/(16 ÷ 2) = 7/8 = 7 ÷ 8 = 0.875.
[WorkedStep] (b)  45/30 = (45 ÷ 15)/(30 ÷ 15) = 3/2 = 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5.
[WorkedStep] (c)  117/26 = (117 ÷ 13)/(26 ÷ 13) = 9/2 = 9 ÷ 2 = 4.5.
[WorkedStep] (d) Keep the whole-number part, 2. Convert the fraction part: 4/20 = (4 ÷ 4)/(20 ÷ 4) = 1/5 = (1 × 2)/(5 × 2) = 2/10 = 0.2. Therefore 2 4/20 = 2 + 0.2 = 2.2.
Revision Question 9
[Question] Convert to fractions in simplest form.
[Question] (a)  0.945
[Question] (b)  3.96
[Question] (c)  0.075
[Question] (d)  −1.45
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) The last digit is in the thousandths place: 0.945 = 945/1000 = (945 ÷ 5)/(1000 ÷ 5) = 189/200.
[WorkedStep] (b) 3.96 = 396/100 = (396 ÷ 4)/(100 ÷ 4) = 99/25 = 3 24/25.
[WorkedStep] (c) 0.075 = 75/1000 = (75 ÷ 25)/(1000 ÷ 25) = 3/40.
[WorkedStep] (d)  The minus sign applies to the whole amount 1.45. First work with its size: 1.45 = 145/100 = (145 ÷ 5)/(100 ÷ 5) = 29/20. Put the minus sign back: −1.45 = −29/20.
[WorkedStep] For a mixed number, 29 = 1 × 20 + 9, so −29/20 = −1 9/20. This notation means −(1 + 9/20), not −1 + 9/20. Check: −1 − 0.45 = −1.45.

Revision Question 10
[Question] Arrange each list in ascending order.
[Question] (a)  3/20, 8 25/100, 0.8215
[Question] (b)  −0.8, 8.1, −8 2/5
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) 3/20 = (3 × 5)/(20 × 5) = 15/100 = 0.15. Also, 8 25/100 = 8 + 0.25 = 8.25. Now compare 0.1500, 0.8215 and 8.2500: 0.15 < 0.8215 < 8.25.
[WorkedStep] Ascending order: 3/20, 0.8215, 8 25/100.
[WorkedStep] (b) 2/5 = (2 × 2)/(5 × 2) = 4/10 = 0.4, so −8 2/5 = −(8 + 0.4) = −8.4. This is 8.4 below zero; −0.8 is only 0.8 below zero. Thus −8.4 < −0.8 < 8.1.
[WorkedStep] Ascending order: −8 2/5, −0.8, 8.1.
Revision Question 11
[Question] Evaluate without a calculator.
[Question] (a)  29.95 + 81.43 + 6.72
[Question] (b)  3.75 + 5.1 + 1.72
[Question] (c)  0.014 + 0.121 + 0.003
[Question] (d)  6.711 × 10
[Question] (e)  (−0.05) × 2
[Question] (f)  (−0.35) × 2
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) Line up the decimal places: 29.95 + 81.43 = 111.38; 111.38 + 6.72 = 118.10 = 118.1.
[WorkedStep] (b)  3.75 + 5.10 = 8.85; 8.85 + 1.72 = 10.57.
[WorkedStep] (c) Line up thousandths: 0.014 + 0.121 = 0.135; 0.135 + 0.003 = 0.138.
[WorkedStep] (d) Multiplying by 10 moves each digit one place left in the place-value chart: 6.711 × 10 = 67.11.
[WorkedStep] (e) (−0.05) × 2 = −0.05 + (−0.05) = −0.10 = −0.1.
[WorkedStep] (f) Similarly, (−0.35) × 2 = −0.35 + (−0.35) = −0.70 = −0.7.

[Question] (b)  4.2 × 8 − 8.8 × 4
[Question] (c)  (5.9 + 5.95) ÷ 3
[Question] (d)  (60.31 − 20.22) ÷ (3 + 5)
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  Bracket: 92 − 2 = 90. Then 1.8 × 90 = 162.
[WorkedStep] (b) Multiply first: 4.2 × 8 = 33.6 and 8.8 × 4 = 35.2. Then subtract: 33.6 − 35.2 = −1.6.
[WorkedStep] (c)  Bracket: 5.90 + 5.95 = 11.85. Then 11.85 ÷ 3 = 3.95.
[WorkedStep] (d)  Brackets: 60.31 − 20.22 = 40.09 and 3 + 5 = 8. Then 40.09 ÷ 8 = 5.01125 ≈ 5.01.
Revision Question 13
[Question] Fill the three boxes in 4.2 □ 8 □ 8.8 □ 4 with +, − and × to get the greatest possible value. Use each operation exactly once.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] We must use +, − and × once each. There are 3 choices for the first box, then 2 unused operations for the second, then 1 for the last. That makes 3 × 2 × 1 = 6 possible arrangements.
[WorkedStep] Let’s check all 6. In each expression, multiply first, then do addition and subtraction from left to right. Keep the numbers 4.2, 8, 8.8 and 4 in their given positions.
[WorkedStep] 4.2 + 8 − 8.8 × 4 = 4.2 + 8 − 35.2 = 12.2 − 35.2 = −23.
[WorkedStep] 4.2 + 8 × 8.8 − 4 = 4.2 + 70.4 − 4 = 70.6.
[WorkedStep] 4.2 − 8 + 8.8 × 4 = 4.2 − 8 + 35.2 = −3.8 + 35.2 = 31.4.
[WorkedStep] 4.2 − 8 × 8.8 + 4 = 4.2 − 70.4 + 4 = −66.2 + 4 = −62.2.
[WorkedStep] 4.2 × 8 + 8.8 − 4 = 33.6 + 8.8 − 4 = 38.4.
[WorkedStep] 4.2 × 8 − 8.8 + 4 = 33.6 − 8.8 + 4 = 28.8.
[WorkedStep] The greatest value is 70.6, using +, ×, − in that order. We have checked all 6 possible arrangements.

[Question] (b)  64.1 × 10²

[WorkedStep] (b)  64.1 × 100 = 6410.
[WorkedStep] (c)  80.3 ÷ 1000 = 0.0803.
[WorkedStep] (d)  77 230 ÷ 10 000 = 7.723.
Revision Question 15
[Question] Mrs Li buys 500 g of flour at $0.28 per 100 g, one packet of sugar for $1.20, and 200 g of butter at $0.49 per 100 g. Find the total cost.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] Flour costs $0.28 for each 100 g. The 500 g of flour contains 500 ÷ 100 = 5 groups of 100 g. Flour cost = 5 × $0.28 = $1.40.
[WorkedStep] Butter costs $0.49 for each 100 g. The 200 g of butter contains 200 ÷ 100 = 2 groups of 100 g. Butter cost = 2 × $0.49 = $0.98.
[WorkedStep] The sugar packet costs $1.20. Add the three costs: $1.40 + $1.20 = $2.60; $2.60 + $0.98 = $3.58. Mrs Li pays $3.58 altogether.
Revision Question 16
[Question] A basket contains 2 kg of apples at $4.20 per kg, 3 kg of grapes at $2.50 per kg and 4 kg of bananas at $1.75 per kg.
[Question] (a)  Find the total mass.
[Question] (b)  Find the total cost.
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  2 + 3 + 4 = 9 kg.
[WorkedStep] (b)  Apples: 2 × $4.20 = $8.40. Grapes: 3 × $2.50 = $7.50. Bananas: 4 × $1.75 = $7.00.
[WorkedStep] Total cost: $8.40 + $7.50 + $7.00 = $22.90.

Revision Question 17
[Question] Express each percentage as a fraction in simplest form.
[Question] (a)  130%
[Question] (b)  25%
[Question] (c)  24.2%
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  130% = 130/100 = (130 ÷ 10)/(100 ÷ 10) = 13/10. This is 13/10 = 1 3/10.
[WorkedStep] (b)  25% = 25/100 = (25 ÷ 25)/(100 ÷ 25) = 1/4.
[WorkedStep] (c)  24.2% = 24.2/100 = (24.2 × 10)/(100 × 10) = 242/1000.
[WorkedStep] Divide both by 2: 242/1000 = (242 ÷ 2)/(1000 ÷ 2) = 121/500.
Revision Question 18
[Question] Convert each percentage to a decimal.
[Question] (a)  11%
[Question] (b)  205%
[Question] (c)  13.6%
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  11% = 11 ÷ 100 = 0.11.
[WorkedStep] (b)  205% = 205 ÷ 100 = 2.05.
[WorkedStep] (c)  13.6% = 13.6 ÷ 100 = 0.136.
Revision Question 19
[Question] Express each as a percentage.
[Question] (a)  3/5
[Question] (b)  2.56
[Question] (c)  0.15
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) 3/5 × 100% = 3 × (100 ÷ 5)% = 3 × 20% = 60%.
[WorkedStep] Keep the % sign: 3/5 equals 60%, not 60.
[WorkedStep] (b)  2.56 × 100% = 256%.
[WorkedStep] (c)  0.15 × 100% = 15%.

[PanelizationLabel] ORIGINAL PANEL CONTENT
We have found percentages such as 5 as a percentage of 10: 5/10 × 100% = 50%. In the next question, the percentage is given and we must find the amount.
Start with 1%. It means 1/100, so divide the full amount by 100. For example, 1% of 80 = 80 ÷ 100 = 0.8. To find 10%, take 10 of those 1% shares: 10 × 0.8 = 8.
We can also write 10% of 80 = 10/100 × 80 = 8. The word “of” asks us to take that fraction of the given amount. Let’s use this method with 5000 and then 600 mL.
Revision Question 20
[Question] Evaluate.
[Question] (a)  30% of 5000
[Question] (b)  45% of 600 mL
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a)  30% means 30 out of 100 equal shares. One share of 5000 is 5000 ÷ 100 = 50. Take 30 shares: 50 × 30 = 1500.
[WorkedStep] So 30% of 5000 = 1500. Check: 1500/5000 = 3/10 = 30%.
[WorkedStep] (b) First find 1% of 600 mL: 600 ÷ 100 = 6 mL. Then take 45 of those shares: 45 × 6 mL = 270 mL.
[WorkedStep] Check: 50% would be 300 mL. Five percent is 5 × 6 = 30 mL, so 45% should be 300 − 30 = 270 mL. It is.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE165-PANEL01

Revision Question 21
[Question] Samuel earns $800 each month and donates $50 to charity. What percentage of his salary does he donate?
Check your method
[WorkedStep] Compare the $50 donation with the full $800 salary: 50/800 × 100% = 5000/800% = 6.25%.
[WorkedStep] Check in money: 1% of $800 is $8. Then 6% is $48, and another 1/4% is $8 ÷ 4 = $2. That makes $50. So Samuel donates 6.25%, or 6 1/4%, of his salary.
Revision Question 22
[Question] William receives a 10% salary increase and Harry receives a 15% salary increase. William concludes, “You will get more money than me.”
[Question] (a)  Do you agree with William’s conclusion? Why?
[Question] (b)  What can you conclude from this?
Check your method
[WorkedStep] (a) We cannot agree without knowing both starting salaries. Let’s test William’s claim with an example.
[WorkedStep] Suppose William starts at $2000 and Harry starts at $1000. These are example salaries, not facts from the question.
[WorkedStep] William’s increase: 10/100 × $2000 = $200. Harry’s increase: 15/100 × $1000 = $150. Here Harry’s 15% increase gives less money than William’s 10% increase, because Harry started with less.
[WorkedStep] Their new salaries would be $2000 + $200 = $2200 and $1000 + $150 = $1150. So the percentages alone tell us neither who gets the larger increase nor who ends with the larger salary.
[WorkedStep] (b) We must know the amount each percentage is taken from. If both starting salaries were $1000, for example, 10% would give $100 and 15% would give $150. With equal starting salaries, the greater percentage gives the greater increase. The question does not say the salaries are equal.
[PanelizationEnd] END PANEL CH02-PAGE166-PANEL01

[PanelizationMetadata] SOURCE: Location CH02 L03 Food Street — Packing Bench and Balanced Loading Table
[PanelizationMetadata] APPLIES TO: CH02-PAGE168-PANEL01; Visual beat CH02 13B A; location reference; geography and equipment at the assigned stage; assigned beat view and state only
[ProductionNote] The upper carrier is a four-by-four arrangement of sixteen cup places. The lower shelf’s MAXIMUM LOAD 4.5 kg label belongs only to that shelf. The table has a fixed pedestal, a rotating head and a centrally pivoted two-tray cradle. Its one accessible brake housing has a rotation latch and a squeeze lever linked to the cradle’s tilt damper. The latch holds rotation from Visual beat CH02 01B C to CH02 13D A; it does not clamp the cradle. Squeezing the lever damps sudden tilt while held; it does not rigidly lock the cradle angle. Mechanical travel stops limit the dip; no tray falls. The original cup drawing is clipped above the bench from Scene CH02 02D until Scene CH02 14A. After dispatch its former clip is empty. Mechanical travel stops limit the dip; no tray falls. The original cup drawing is clipped above the bench from Scene CH02 02D until Scene CH02 14A. After dispatch its former clip is empty. Use exact dedicated count diagrams for the pack states; do not demand tiny exact counts in every scenic wide.

[SceneHeading] Scene CH02 14B Everyone in the first group receives a drink
[ProductionLabel] Production instructions are non-printing. Exact reader text is assigned beneath each visual beat.
[ProductionNote] Setting. Location CH02 L04: Outside the Old Blue Gate, two weathered blue timber leaves stand between pale-stone piers, with brass ribs, moon-shaped openings and one round full-moon ornament above. Seen from the lane, the small service doorway is in the left leaf, the bench is right and the planter is left. Same full-moon night. Warm task lamps and cool moonlit edges remain consistent; the current scene controls repaired and unrepaired states.
[ProductionNote] View. Exterior medium at the service doorway, bench right and planter left as viewed from the waiting lane.
[ProductionNote] Cast and positions. Outside the Gate, Ira stands nearest the small service doorway in the left leaf as seen from the lane; Kabir stands beside her with his ruled notebook. The girl in green waits with her two friends close to them. The green Gate helper controls the doorway. Other waiting children remain behind the group; no parent or human stall worker is present.
[ProductionNote] Props and state progression. The large blue doors remain shut to general admission until the final authorisation. The small service doorway permits supervised messages and food delivery. The separate equipment exit beyond the left pier is not this door. Food-delivery groups do not determine admission groups. Ira’s cup drawing and each later written message are separate sheets. The broad helper has brought the same loaded trolley from Return Walk through Entry Court to the supervised service doorway. The first sixteen names are on Kabir’s list. The original cup drawing is clipped to the trolley; the first-trip tag remains attached.
[ProductionNote] Planning requirements. The first drink group includes Ira, Kabir and the girl in green, but their admission group will be the later twenty-two. Serving does not trigger admission.

[ProductionNote] Source issues and editorial decisions
[ProductionNote] Earlier corrections retained and checked: Key Ideas uses 4/9 ÷ 2/3 = 2/3, and Practice 2H Question 6 uses the source name Abdul.
[ProductionNote] Practice 2C Question 3(b), printed 45; answer key 362. The expression is 4/5 − 2/3 ÷ 4/8. Division gives 4/3; subtraction gives 12/15 -20/15 = -8/15. The supplied key prints+8/15. This draft teaches−8/15, checked independently.
[ProductionNote] Recurring-decimal note, printed 46. The source calls every non-terminating decimal recurring. The draft defines recurring as having a repeating digit/block. It does not claim that all infinite decimals repeat.
[ProductionNote] Improper fraction, printed 31. The source’s introductory sentence describes numerator greater than denominator. The draft also includes equality, for example 4/4=1, and distinguishes division by 1 from division by a fraction greater than 1.
[ProductionNote] Practice 2E Question 7 and 8(b); key 363. The source asks about pears; the key says mangoes. The draft retains pears. Part 8(b) asks descending order, whereas the key’s last line repeats ascending order. The draft gives descending order and explains it using twentieths.
[ProductionNote] Practice 2I Question 2; key 363. The question gives no rounding requirement. The draft supplies exact values−8/3 for(a–c) and−188/61 for(d), with the key’s one-decimal approximations identified as approximations. It rejects the key’s overbroad claim that order does not matter for multiplication/division.
[ProductionNote] Practice 2L Question 7; key 364. The intended answer uses 1000 as the total by treating pet categories as separate groups. The question does not explicitly rule out overlapping families. The draft states the assumption and explains that an overlapping survey would need a distinct-family total. The difference 25%−15% is described as 10 percentage points.
[ProductionNote] Self-check, printed 87–88. The source assigns 4 points to Question 15(a,b) and 16(a,b), although Question 15 has no subparts. Its category scores sum to 65 while the printed total is 61. This draft uses Question 15 and 16(a,b), worth 3, and a consistent overall total 64. This is an editorial correction, not a claim of prior author approval.
[ProductionNote] Savings comparison, printed 80–81. Preserved the values and percentage comparison. Replaced the personal judgement “thriftier” with the supported statement that Linda saves the larger percentage of her income.
[ProductionNote] Sweets spreadsheet, printed 75. Preserved the task and demonstration values. Clarified incomplete entries and exact stored values versus rounded displays. Use =B$3/$F$1 so copying down retains count row 3 and copying across retains total F1. This also corrects Draft 07’s copy-down instruction. Real observations must be supplied by the learner; none have been invented.
[ProductionNote] Rounding notation and decimal precision. Used≈ when rounding changes a value and preserved requested trailing zeros. Monetary source symbols and numerical values remain dollars/cents; these were not silently localised to rupees.
[ProductionNote] Visuals are mathematical teaching drawings, not final graphic-novel artwork. They use clear teaching colours and exact partitions, counts and scales; each has a nearby instruction to apply current ChandRush styling only where it preserves comprehension. Essential question diagrams remain unsolved, with solution figures separated. A later layout must preserve that separation. No essential visual is intentionally left as a placeholder.
